statement: Let $X$ solve the [stochastic differential equation](c:stochastic-differential-equation) $dX_t = b(X_t)\,dt + \sigma(X_t)\,dW_t$ in an open interval $I$. Let $V$ be a [continuously differentiable](c:continuously-differentiable-map) function on $I$ that is $C^2$ off a finite set $F$ where $\sigma \ne 0$, and that solves $\min\{\mathcal L V - \lambda V + w,\ z - V\} = 0$ off $F$. Then the exit time $\tau^*$ of $X$ from $D = \{V < z\}$ minimizes $J[\tau] = E[\int_0^\tau e^{-\lambda s} w(X_s)\,ds + e^{-\lambda\tau} z(X_\tau)]$ over the finite [stopping times](c:stopping-time) $\tau$ for which the [Itô integral](c:ito-integral) $\int_0^\tau e^{-\lambda s} V'(X_s)\sigma(X_s)\,dW_s$ has mean zero, if $\tau^*$ is one of them and $E|V(X_0)| < \infty$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a continuous solution of $dX_t = b(X_t)\,dt + \sigma(X_t)\,dW_t$ that stays in the open interval $I$, with $b$ and $\sigma$ continuous.
$V$ is $C^1$ on $I$ and $C^2$ on $I \setminus F$ for a finite set $F$, $V''$ is bounded near $F$, and $\sigma \ne 0$ on $F$.
$\min\{\mathcal L V - \lambda V + w,\ z - V\} = 0$ on $I \setminus F$, with $w$ and $z$ continuous and $\lambda \ge 0$.
$E|V(X_0)| < \infty$, and $\tau^*$ is a.s. finite with $E\int_0^{\tau^*} e^{-\lambda s} V'(X_s)\sigma(X_s)\,dW_s = 0$.

conclusion: $J[\tau^*] = E\,V(X_0) \le J[\tau]$ for every admissible $\tau$, so $E\,V(X_0)$ is the optimal cost and $V$ is the [value function](c:value-function) of the problem.

proofs.name: Relaxed Itô rule and comparison
proofs.slogan: Extend Itô's rule to the $C^1$ function $V$, then compare its expansion with the cost of any rule for the [optimal stopping problem](c:optimal-stopping-problem).
proofs.scope: The full statement. The Itô rule is proved for finitely many points where $V$ is only $C^1$, not for a general measurable second derivative.

roles.why: The equation and the continuity of the coefficients give Itô's formula and the bounds after localization.
A $C^1$ function with a bounded second derivative off $F$ is a limit of $C^2$ functions, and $\sigma \ne 0$ on $F$ makes the time at $F$ negligible.
The two inequalities give the lower bound, and the equation inside $D$ gives the equality for $\tau^*$.
A mean-zero stochastic integral and an integrable $V(X_0)$ make the expansion of $V$ have mean $E\,V(X_0)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the diffusion spends zero time at each point where $\sigma \ne 0$.
steps.detail: Itô's formula for $F_\varepsilon$ with $F_\varepsilon'' = g_\varepsilon \ge 1_{\{a\}}$ and $|F_\varepsilon'| \le 4\varepsilon$ bounds $\tfrac12\sigma(a)^2$ times the [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) of $\{s \le t : X_s = a\}$ by terms that tend to zero.

steps.slogan: Approximate $V$ by $C^2$ functions whose second derivatives equal $V''$ away from $F$.
steps.detail: Replace $V''$ by a linear interpolation on $[a - 1/n, a + 1/n]$ for each $a \in F$ and integrate twice. The approximations converge to $V$ with their first derivatives, uniformly on compact sets.

steps.slogan: Pass to the limit in Itô's formula for the approximations to get Itô's rule for $V$.
steps.detail: The second-derivative terms converge at almost every time because the time spent at $F$ is null, and the stochastic integrals converge in $L^2$ by the Itô isometry.

steps.slogan: Bound the cost of every admissible rule below by the mean of $V(X_0)$.
steps.detail: The expansion $Y_\tau = V(X_0) + M_\tau$ has mean $E\,V(X_0)$, and $V \le z$ and $\lambda V - \mathcal L V \le w$ give $Y_\tau \le Z_\tau$, the realized cost of $\tau$.

steps.slogan: Show that the exit rule from the continuation region turns both bounds into equalities.
steps.detail: Before $\tau^*$ the process is in $D$, where $\mathcal L V - \lambda V + w = 0$, and at $\tau^*$ it is in the closed set $\{V = z\}$, so $Y_{\tau^*} = Z_{\tau^*}$.

concepts.c:stochastic-differential-equation: The state of the stopping problem is the solution of a one-dimensional stochastic differential equation.
concepts.c:continuously-differentiable-map: Smooth fit means that V is continuously differentiable across the boundary of the continuation region.
concepts.c:stopping-time: The controller chooses a stopping time, and the theorem compares all admissible stopping times.
concepts.c:ito-integral: The mean-zero condition on the Itô integral defines the admissible class of stopping times.
concepts.c:value-function: The theorem identifies the solution of the variational inequality with the value function.
concepts.c:optimal-stopping-problem: The cost J is the objective of an optimal stopping problem for a diffusion.
concepts.c:lebesgue-measure: The time spent at the points of F has Lebesgue measure zero, so V'' is not needed there.

new_concepts.name: optimal stopping problem
new_concepts.reminder: An optimal stopping problem asks for a stopping time that maximizes the expected reward of stopping a random process.
new_concepts.definition: Let $(Z_n)_{0\le n\le N}$, with $N\le\infty$, be integrable rewards adapted to a [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal{F}_n)$. The optimal stopping problem asks for the [expected value](c:expected-value) $V=\sup_\tau\mathbb{E}[Z_\tau]$ over all [stopping times](c:stopping-time) $\tau\le N$, with $\tau<\infty$ almost surely when $N=\infty$, and for an optimal $\tau^*$ with $\mathbb{E}[Z_{\tau^*}]=V$. Because $\tau$ is a stopping time, each decision to stop uses only the information available at that time.

statement: In the Black-Scholes model with $r > 0$, the perpetual American put has price $V(x) = K - x$ for $x \le L^*$ and $V(x) = (K - L^*)(x/L^*)^{-2r/\sigma^2}$ for $x \ge L^*$, where $L^* = 2rK/(2r + \sigma^2)$. The first [stopping time](c:stopping-time) at which the price reaches $L^*$ is optimal for this [optimal stopping problem](c:optimal-stopping-problem).

hypotheses.text: The interest rate $r$, the volatility $\sigma$ and the strike $K$ are strictly positive.
Under $P^*$, $S_t = x\exp(\sigma B_t + (r - \sigma^2/2)t)$ with a standard [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $B$.
Exercise at a [stopping time](c:stopping-time) $\tau$ pays $(K - S_\tau)^+$ at time $\tau$, and no exercise pays $0$.

conclusion: $\sup_\tau \mathbb{E}^*[e^{-r\tau}(K - S_\tau)^+] = V(x)$ for every $x > 0$, and $\tau^* = \inf\{t : S_t \le L^*\}$ attains it.

proofs.name: Verification of the smooth-fit candidate
proofs.slogan: Show that the discounted candidate is a [supermartingale](c:supermartingale) above the payoff, and that it is a [martingale](c:martingale) until the price first reaches $L^*$.
proofs.scope: The value for every initial price and the optimality of $\tau^*$, for $r > 0$. The case $r = 0$ is excluded.

roles.why: Positive rates make $\gamma > 0$ and $L^* < K$, and the discount factor kills the payoff at $\tau = \infty$.
The model gives the generator for Itô's formula and the exponential martingale $e^{-rt}S_t^{-\gamma}$.
The payoff convention fixes the gain that the supermartingale bound must dominate.

steps.slogan: Check that the candidate $V$ is $C^1$, [convex](c:convex-function) and above the payoff.
steps.detail: Both branches have slope $-1$ at $L^*$, which is smooth fit. Convexity puts $V$ above its tangent $K - x$. The generator gives $-rK$ below $L^*$ and $0$ above $L^*$.

steps.slogan: Prove that $e^{-rt}V(S_t)$ is a [supermartingale](c:supermartingale) with Itô's formula after mollification.
steps.detail: In log coordinates the candidate has a Lipschitz derivative. A [mollifier](c:mollifier) gives smooth functions with nonpositive generator. Itô's formula and the martingale property of the stochastic integral give supermartingales, and the uniform limit keeps the property.

steps.slogan: Bound the discounted payoff of every exercise rule by $V(x)$ with optional stopping.
steps.detail: Optional stopping at $\tau \wedge t$ and dominated convergence as $t \to \infty$ give $\mathbb{E}^*[e^{-r\tau}V(S_\tau)] \le V(x)$. The payoff is at most $V$.

steps.slogan: Compute the payoff of $\tau^*$ with the exponential [martingale](c:martingale) $e^{-rt}S_t^{-\gamma}$.
steps.detail: Stopped at $\tau^*$ this martingale is bounded by $(L^*)^{-\gamma}$. Optional stopping and dominated convergence give $\mathbb{E}^*[e^{-r\tau^*}] = (x/L^*)^{-\gamma}$, so $\tau^*$ pays $V(x)$.

steps.slogan: Join the two bounds to identify the value of the [optimal stopping problem](c:optimal-stopping-problem).
steps.detail: The upper bound holds for every stopping time and $\tau^*$ attains it. So the price is $V(x)$ and $\tau^*$ is an optimal exercise rule.

concepts.c:stopping-time: Exercise rules are stopping times, and the optimal one is a hitting time.
concepts.c:optimal-stopping-problem: The option price is the value of an optimal stopping problem with discounting.
concepts.c:brownian-motion: The asset price is the exponential of a Brownian motion with drift.
concepts.c:supermartingale: The discounted candidate value is a supermartingale, which bounds every exercise rule.
concepts.c:martingale: The exponential martingale of the price computes the discounted payoff of the hitting time.
concepts.c:convex-function: Convexity of the candidate puts it above the payoff line K minus x.
concepts.c:mollifier: Mollification smooths the candidate so that Itô's formula applies at the exercise boundary.

new_concepts.name: supermartingale
new_concepts.reminder: A supermartingale is an adapted integrable process whose conditional mean of the next value is at most the present value.
new_concepts.definition: An adapted process $(X_n)$ of [integrable](c:integrable-function) random variables for a [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ is a supermartingale when the [conditional expectation](c:conditional-expectation) satisfies $\mathbb{E}[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_n]\le X_n$ almost surely for every $n$. In continuous time the condition is $\mathbb{E}[X_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s]\le X_s$ for $s\le t$. So a supermartingale decreases on average, and $-X$ is a [submartingale](c:submartingale).

statement: Let $P \ne Q$ and let $X_1, X_2, \dots$ be [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables) with law $P$ or $Q$. The sequential probability ratio test $\psi$ stops at the first $n$ with $r_n \le A$ or $r_n \ge B$, where $r_n$ is the product of the [likelihood ratios](c:radon-nikodym-derivative) $f(X_j)$ and $0 < A < 1 < B < \infty$. Every sequential test $\varphi$ whose error probabilities are at most those of $\psi$, and whose sample size $N_\varphi$ (a [stopping time](c:stopping-time)) has finite mean under $P$ and $Q$, satisfies $E_P N_\psi \le E_P N_\varphi$ and $E_Q N_\psi \le E_Q N_\varphi$.

hypotheses.text: The laws $P$ and $Q$ are distinct.
Under either law the observations are [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables).
The thresholds satisfy $0 < A < 1 < B < \infty$.
The test $\varphi$, possibly randomized, has $\alpha_P(\varphi) \le \alpha_P(\psi)$, $\alpha_Q(\varphi) \le \alpha_Q(\psi)$ and finite $E_P N_\varphi$ and $E_Q N_\varphi$.

conclusion: $E_P N_\psi \le E_P N_\varphi$ and $E_Q N_\psi \le E_Q N_\varphi$, and both means for $\psi$ are finite.

proofs.name: Embedding in a Bayes problem
proofs.slogan: Find costs and a prior near 0 or 1 that make the SPRT minimize the [Bayes risk](c:bayes-risk), then compare risks and let the prior tend to the boundary.
proofs.scope: Outline of the proof in Dudley's notes for competing tests with finite mean sample sizes (Case I of the source). The lemmas on the Bayes risk are cited, not proved.

roles.why: Distinct laws make the log-likelihood walk move, which gives the geometric tail of the sample size and small risks for small cost.
Independence lets a test restart after one observation with the posterior as the new prior, and makes the blocks of the walk independent.
Thresholds on both sides of 1 can be matched with posterior thresholds for a prior strictly between them.
Smaller error probabilities and finite means make the risk difference reduce to the mean sample sizes.

steps.slogan: Bound the tail of the SPRT sample size by a geometric sequence.
steps.detail: Blocks of $m$ observations whose log-likelihood increment exceeds $\log(B/A)$ in absolute value have probability at least $p^m > 0$, so $\mu(N_\psi > im) \le (1 - p^m)^i$ for $\mu = P, Q$.

steps.slogan: Write the Bayes risk as a minimum of three risks and split it over the first observation.
steps.detail: The risk $r(p, \varphi)$ is affine in the prior, so the infimum $r(p)$ over tests that observe is [concave](c:concave-function) and $R(p) = \min(pv, r(p), (1 - p)w)$. Lemma 1.7.1 writes the risk as $c$ plus the mean posterior risk.

steps.slogan: Find posterior thresholds $p_L \le p_U$ and the Bellman equation between them.
steps.detail: The roots of $r(p) = pv$ and $r(p) = (1 - p)w$ give $p_L$ and $p_U$, and Proposition 1.7.6 proves $R(p) = c + \int R(p_x)\, d(pP + qQ)(x)$ for $p_L < p < p_U$. This is the Bellman equation of an [optimal stopping problem](c:optimal-stopping-problem).

steps.slogan: Show that the SPRT with matching thresholds attains the Bayes risk.
steps.detail: Posterior thresholds $p_U$ and $p_L$ correspond to $r_n \le A(p)$ and $r_n \ge B(p)$. Induction with the Bellman equation bounds the risk on stopped paths, and dominated convergence removes the rest.

steps.slogan: Choose cost and loss so that the given SPRT is Bayes for a prior near 0 or near 1.
steps.detail: Continuity of $p_L$ and $p_U$ in the cost and the intermediate value theorem give $j(c) = A/B$, and then a prior $p < \varepsilon$, or $p > 1 - \varepsilon$, with $A(p) = A$ and $B(p) = B$.

steps.slogan: Compare the Bayes risks of the SPRT and the competing test and let the prior tend to the boundary.
steps.detail: The error terms are at most zero, so $p\,d_P + q\,d_Q \ge 0$ for the differences of the mean sample sizes. Letting $p \to 0$ gives $d_Q \ge 0$, and $q \to 0$ gives $d_P \ge 0$.

concepts.c:iid-random-variables: Independent observations let the test restart after each observation with an updated prior.
concepts.c:radon-nikodym-derivative: The likelihood ratio of Q to P is the density that the SPRT multiplies along the sample.
concepts.c:stopping-time: The sample size of a sequential test is a stopping time of the observations and the randomization.
concepts.c:bayes-risk: The SPRT is shown to minimize the Bayes risk for suitable costs, losses and prior.
concepts.c:concave-function: The minimum risk of tests that observe is concave in the prior, which gives unique thresholds.
concepts.c:optimal-stopping-problem: Choosing when to stop sampling is an optimal stopping problem for the posterior probability.

statement: For [independent](c:independent-random-variables) nonnegative rewards $X_1, X_2, \dots$, a player who sees all values in advance gains at most twice what the best [stopping time](c:stopping-time) gains: $\mathbb{E}\sup_n X_n \le 2 \sup_N \mathbb{E}X_N$. A single threshold at a [median](c:median) of the maximum attains half of the prophet value.

hypotheses.text: The rewards $X_1, X_2, \dots$ are [independent](c:independent-random-variables).
Each $X_i$ is nonnegative, and for finitely many rewards each $X_i$ is integrable.
The player uses a [stopping time](c:stopping-time) $N$ of the observations, finite almost surely.

conclusion: $\mathbb{E}\max_{j \le n} X_j \le 2\,\mathbb{E}X_\tau$ for a threshold rule $\tau$ at a median $m$ of the maximum, and $\mathbb{E}\sup_n X_n \le 2\sup_N \mathbb{E}X_N$.

proofs.name: Samuel-Cahn median threshold
proofs.slogan: Compare the prophet value $m + \beta$ with the gain of a threshold rule at a [median](c:median) $m$ of the maximum.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Two threshold rules cover the cases $m \le \beta$ and $m \ge \beta$. Monotone convergence gives the infinite sequence.

roles.why: The event that the rule is still running at time $i$ depends only on earlier rewards, so it is independent of $X_i$.
A rule that never meets the threshold still gains $X_n \ge 0$, and the median is nonnegative.
The threshold rules are stopping times, so their gains are lower bounds for the stopping value.

steps.slogan: Bound the prophet value by the median plus the expected total excess.
steps.detail: The excess of the maximum over $m$ is the largest excess $(X_i - m)^+$, which is at most their sum. So $\mathbb{E}M_n \le m + \beta$ with $\beta = \sum_i \mathbb{E}(X_i - m)^+$.

steps.slogan: Split the excess of a threshold rule over the times at which it is still running.
steps.detail: For a threshold rule $\tau$ at level $m$, $(X_\tau - m)^+ = \sum_i (X_i - m)^+ 1\{\tau \ge i\}$. The event $\{\tau \ge i\}$ depends on $X_1, \dots, X_{i-1}$ only, so $\mathbb{E}(X_\tau - m)^+ = \sum_i \mathbb{E}(X_i - m)^+ P(\tau \ge i)$.

steps.slogan: For $m \le \beta$, the strict threshold rule $s(m)$ gains at least $(m + \beta)/2$.
steps.detail: Each $P(s(m) \ge i)$ is at least $P(M_n \le m) = 1 - p$, and $X_{s(m)} > m$ exactly when $M_n > m$. So $\mathbb{E}X_{s(m)} \ge \beta(1-p) + mp \ge (m+\beta)/2$ because $p \le 1/2$.

steps.slogan: For $m \ge \beta$, the weak threshold rule $t(m)$ gains at least $(m + \beta)/2$.
steps.detail: Each $P(t(m) \ge i)$ is at least $P(M_n < m) = q$, and $X_{t(m)} \ge m$ exactly when $M_n \ge m$. So $\mathbb{E}X_{t(m)} \ge \beta q + m(1-q) \ge (m+\beta)/2$ because $q \le 1/2$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two cases and let the horizon grow by monotone convergence.
steps.detail: In both cases a stopping time gains at least $(m+\beta)/2 \ge \mathbb{E}M_n/2$. For an infinite sequence with integrable terms, $\mathbb{E}M_n \uparrow \mathbb{E}\sup_n X_n$, which gives the bound for the [optimal stopping problem](c:optimal-stopping-problem) over finite stopping times.

concepts.c:independent-random-variables: Independence makes the running event of a rule independent of the current reward.
concepts.c:stopping-time: The player may only use stopping times, which see the past and not the future.
concepts.c:median: The threshold of the rule is a median of the maximum reward.
concepts.c:optimal-stopping-problem: The stopping value is the value of an optimal stopping problem.

statement: In a discounted bandit with independent arms that are [Markov chains](c:markov-chain) and that move only when played, the policy that always plays an arm of largest Gittins index is optimal. The index of a state is the best discounted reward rate up to a [stopping time](c:stopping-time) $\tau \ge 1$.

hypotheses.text: The arms are independent [Markov chains](c:markov-chain) on countable state spaces, and an arm changes its state only when it is played.
The rewards $r_i$ are bounded and discounted by $\alpha^{t-1}$ with $\alpha \in (0,1)$.
A policy chooses each arm from the past and present states, the past actions and an independent randomization.

conclusion: Every Gittins index policy $\pi^*$ satisfies $V(\pi^*) = \sup_\pi V(\pi)$, where $V(\pi) = \mathbb{E}\sum_{t \ge 1} \alpha^{t-1} r_{A_t}(S_{A_t}(t))$.

proofs.name: Prevailing charge proof
proofs.slogan: Charge each play the running minimum of the arm's index: no policy beats these charges, and the index policy collects them greedily in decreasing order.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for countable state spaces, bounded rewards and randomized policies. General reward sequences are not treated.

roles.why: Independence and the Markov property give the conditional law of the next state, and frozen arms make the telescoping and the greedy order work.
Discounting makes the calibration map a contraction and lets the discounted sums converge.
Non-anticipating choices make each play event known at the time of the play, which the conditional step needs.

steps.slogan: Calibrate one arm against a retirement charge $\gamma$ with the fixed point $v_\gamma$.
steps.detail: The [contraction mapping](c:contraction-mapping) $f \mapsto \max(0, r - \gamma + \alpha P f)$ has a fixed point $v_\gamma$. A [supermartingale](c:supermartingale) and a stopped [martingale](c:martingale) show $v_\gamma(x) = 0$ exactly when $g(x) \le \gamma$, and $v_\gamma = r - \gamma + \alpha P v_\gamma$ when $g(x) \ge \gamma$.

steps.slogan: Bound the discounted rewards of each arm by its discounted prevailing charges.
steps.detail: On each block of plays at a fixed prevailing charge $\gamma_j$, the net reward equals a telescoping sum of $v_{\gamma_j}$ terms. It starts at $v_{\gamma_j} = 0$ and has only nonpositive later terms, so its mean is at most $0$.

steps.slogan: Show that the index policy plays each block to its end, which gives equality.
steps.detail: After the index policy chooses an arm at charge $\gamma_j$, the arm keeps the strictly largest index until its index falls to $\gamma_j$. So the block has consecutive plays and the telescoping sum is exactly $0$.

steps.slogan: Show that the index policy always plays an arm with largest prevailing charge.
steps.detail: The prevailing charge of the chosen arm is the index of a state in which the policy chose that arm earlier. At that time it was at least every other index, and charges only decrease.

steps.slogan: Prove that the greedy interleaving of nonincreasing sequences maximizes every discounted sum.
steps.detail: An exchange argument shows that the greedy prefix of each length has the largest sum. Abel summation with weights $(1-\alpha)\alpha^{m-1}$ turns the prefix bounds into the discounted bound.

steps.slogan: Compare every policy with the index policy through the policy-free greedy value of the charges.
steps.detail: The charge sequences depend only on the chains. Every policy earns at most the greedy discounted charge value, and the index policy earns exactly that value.

concepts.c:markov-chain: Each arm is a Markov chain that moves only when the policy plays it.
concepts.c:stopping-time: The Gittins index is a best reward rate over stopping times of a single arm.
concepts.c:contraction-mapping: The calibration function is the fixed point of a contraction on bounded functions.
concepts.c:supermartingale: The calibration function bounds every stopped profit through a supermartingale.
concepts.c:martingale: Stopped at the first zero of the calibration function, the profit process is a martingale.

new_concepts.definition: An adapted process $(X_n)$ of [integrable](c:integrable-function) random variables for a [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ is a supermartingale when the [conditional expectation](c:conditional-expectation) satisfies $\mathbb{E}[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_n]\le X_n$ almost surely for every $n$. In continuous time the condition is $\mathbb{E}[X_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s]\le X_s$ for $s\le t$. So a supermartingale decreases on average, and $-X$ is a [submartingale](c:submartingale).

statement: For a geometric change point and i.i.d. observations before and after the change, the [stopping time](c:stopping-time) that raises an alarm when the posterior [conditional probability](c:conditional-probability) $p_n = P(\Gamma \le n \mid X_1, \dots, X_n)$ first reaches a threshold $A_\alpha$ minimizes $\mathbb{E}(\tau - \Gamma)^+$ among all rules with $P(\tau < \Gamma) \le \alpha$, when $A_\alpha$ gives false alarm probability exactly $\alpha$.

hypotheses.text: The change point $\Gamma$ is geometric: $P(\Gamma = n) = \rho(1 - \rho)^{n-1}$ for $n \ge 1$.
Given $\Gamma$, the observations are independent with density $f_0$ before $\Gamma$ and $f_1$ from $\Gamma$ on, and $0 < D(f_1 \| f_0) < \infty$.
The threshold $A_\alpha \in (0,1)$ gives the Shiryaev rule a false alarm probability exactly $\alpha$.

conclusion: $\tau_S = \inf\{n \ge 1 : p_n \ge A_\alpha\}$ minimizes $\mathrm{ADD}(\tau)$ over all stopping times with $\mathrm{PFA}(\tau) \le \alpha$.

proofs.name: Lagrangian relaxation and dynamic programming
proofs.slogan: Relax the false alarm constraint with a multiplier, solve the relaxed [optimal stopping problem](c:optimal-stopping-problem) on the posterior, and read a threshold off a concave [value function](c:value-function).
proofs.scope: Outline of the proof sketch in the source. The existence of the multiplier, the dynamic programming equation and the concavity are cited, not proved.

roles.why: The geometric prior makes the posterior recursion time-homogeneous, so dynamic programming has a stationary value function.
Independence given the change point gives the Bayes recursion and the Markov property of the posterior.
An exact false alarm level makes the relaxed solution feasible and optimal for the constrained problem.

steps.slogan: Update the posterior probability of a change by Bayes' rule.
steps.detail: The recursion $p_{n+1} = \tilde p_n L(X_{n+1}) / (\tilde p_n L(X_{n+1}) + 1 - \tilde p_n)$ with $\tilde p_n = p_n + (1 - p_n)\rho$ makes $(p_n)$ a [Markov chain](c:markov-chain) and a sufficient statistic.

steps.slogan: Write the delay and the false alarm probability as expectations of the posterior.
steps.detail: Because $\{n < \tau\}$ depends only on the first $n$ observations, $\mathrm{ADD}(\tau) = \mathbb{E}\sum_{n<\tau} p_n$ and $\mathrm{PFA}(\tau) = \mathbb{E}[1 - p_\tau]$.

steps.slogan: Relax the constraint with a multiplier $\lambda_f$ and show that an exact-level solution is constrained optimal.
steps.detail: If $\tau_\lambda$ minimizes $\mathrm{ADD} + \lambda_f \mathrm{PFA}$ and has level $\alpha$, then every rule of level at most $\alpha$ has delay at least $\mathrm{ADD}(\tau_\lambda)$. The source cites Shiryaev for the existence of $\lambda_f$.

steps.slogan: Solve the relaxed problem with the Bellman equation on the posterior.
steps.detail: The [value function](c:value-function) satisfies $J(p) = \min\{\lambda_f(1 - p), p + A_J(p)\}$. The source states that $J$ and $A_J$ are concave with $J(1) = A_J(1) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Read off a threshold [stopping time](c:stopping-time) from the concave cost difference.
steps.detail: The difference $p + A_J(p) - \lambda_f(1-p)$ is concave and positive at $p = 1$, so the stopping set is an interval $[A, 1]$. With the multiplier of the relaxation, $A = A_\alpha$.

concepts.c:stopping-time: An alarm rule is a stopping time of the observation sequence.
concepts.c:conditional-probability: The Shiryaev statistic is the posterior probability that the change has happened.
concepts.c:optimal-stopping-problem: The relaxed problem is an optimal stopping problem for the posterior process.
concepts.c:value-function: Concavity of the value function gives the threshold form of the optimal rule.
concepts.c:markov-chain: The posterior evolves as a Markov chain, so it is a sufficient state for dynamic programming.

source.ref: V. V. Veeravalli and T. Banerjee, Quickest Change Detection, arXiv:1210.5552, Theorem 3.1 and its proof, pp. 11-12.
source.note: The source gives a proof sketch and cites Shiryaev (1963, 1978) for the details. The steps follow the sketch and add the elementary identities for the costs and the Lagrange argument.

new_concepts.name: optimal stopping problem
new_concepts.reminder: An optimal stopping problem asks for a stopping time that maximizes the expected reward of stopping a random process.
new_concepts.definition: Let $(Z_n)_{0\le n\le N}$, with $N\le\infty$, be integrable rewards adapted to a [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal{F}_n)$. The optimal stopping problem asks for the [expected value](c:expected-value) $V=\sup_\tau\mathbb{E}[Z_\tau]$ over all [stopping times](c:stopping-time) $\tau\le N$, with $\tau<\infty$ almost surely when $N=\infty$, and for an optimal $\tau^*$ with $\mathbb{E}[Z_{\tau^*}]=V$. Because $\tau$ is a stopping time, each decision to stop uses only the information available at that time.

statement: For [i.i.d.](c:iid-random-variables) steps $X_i$ with mean $\mu$ and a [stopping time](c:stopping-time) $N$ with $\mathbb{E}N < \infty$, the stopped sum satisfies $\mathbb{E}S_N = \mu\,\mathbb{E}N$. If the [variance](c:variance) $\sigma^2$ is finite, then also $\mathbb{E}(S_N - \mu N)^2 = \sigma^2\,\mathbb{E}N$.

hypotheses.text: The steps $X_1, X_2, \dots$ are [i.i.d.](c:iid-random-variables) with $\mathbb{E}|X_1| < \infty$ and $\mu = \mathbb{E}X_1$.
For each $n \ge 1$, $X_n$ is $\mathcal{F}_n$-measurable and [independent](c:independent-random-variables) of $\mathcal{F}_{n-1}$ for the [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal{F}_n)$.
$N$ is a [stopping time](c:stopping-time) for $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ with values in $\{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ and $\mathbb{E}N < \infty$.
For the second identity: $\sigma^2 = \operatorname{Var} X_1 < \infty$.

conclusion: $\mathbb{E}S_N = \mu\,\mathbb{E}N$, and $\mathbb{E}(S_N - \mu N)^2 = \sigma^2\,\mathbb{E}N$ when $\sigma^2 < \infty$.

proofs.name: Series over the events N at least m
proofs.slogan: Write the stopped [random walk](c:random-walk) as a series over the events $\{N \ge m\}$, which are independent of the step $X_m$.
proofs.scope: Both identities. The first follows Proof #1 of the source. The second is an $L^2$ version of the same series argument.

roles.why: Identical means turn each term $\mathbb{E}[X_m 1\{N \ge m\}]$ into $\mu P(N \ge m)$.
Independence of $X_m$ from $\mathcal{F}_{m-1}$ splits the expectations and kills the cross terms.
The stopping property puts $\{N \ge m\}$ in $\mathcal{F}_{m-1}$, and $\mathbb{E}N < \infty$ makes the series converge.
A finite variance makes each diagonal term equal to $\sigma^2 P(N \ge m)$.

steps.slogan: Write the stopped sum as a series over the events $\{N \ge m\}$.
steps.detail: On the event $N < \infty$, which has probability one, $S_N = \sum_{m \ge 1} X_m 1\{N \ge m\}$. The tail sum formula gives $\sum_m P(N \ge m) = \mathbb{E}N < \infty$.

steps.slogan: Each event $\{N \ge m\}$ is independent of the step $X_m$.
steps.detail: The event $\{N \ge m\}$ is the complement of $\{N \le m-1\}$, so it is in $\mathcal{F}_{m-1}$. Hence $\mathbb{E}[X_m 1\{N \ge m\}] = \mu P(N \ge m)$ and $\mathbb{E}[|X_m| 1\{N \ge m\}] = \mathbb{E}|X_1| P(N \ge m)$.

steps.slogan: Swap expectation and sum to get the [expected value](c:expected-value) of the stopped sum.
steps.detail: Tonelli gives $\mathbb{E}\sum_m |X_m| 1\{N \ge m\} = \mathbb{E}|X_1|\,\mathbb{E}N < \infty$, so $S_N$ is integrable. Fubini then gives $\mathbb{E}S_N = \sum_m \mu P(N \ge m) = \mu\,\mathbb{E}N$.

steps.slogan: Compute the second moment of the centred sum stopped at a fixed time.
steps.detail: With $T_n = S_n - n\mu$, the increment $T_{N\wedge n} - T_{N\wedge k}$ equals $\sum_{m=k+1}^{n} (X_m - \mu) 1\{N \ge m\}$. Cross terms vanish because $X_j - \mu$ has mean zero and is independent of $\mathcal{F}_{j-1}$. So $\mathbb{E}(T_{N\wedge n} - T_{N\wedge k})^2 = \sigma^2\,\mathbb{E}(N\wedge n - N\wedge k)$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the limit in $L^2$ with Fatou's lemma and monotone convergence.
steps.detail: Fatou's lemma gives $\mathbb{E}(T_N - T_{N\wedge n})^2 \le \sigma^2 \sum_{m > n} P(N \ge m) \to 0$. So $\mathbb{E}T_{N\wedge n}^2 \to \mathbb{E}T_N^2$, while $\mathbb{E}(N \wedge n) \uparrow \mathbb{E}N$. Hence $\mathbb{E}T_N^2 = \sigma^2\,\mathbb{E}N$.

steps.slogan: Collect Wald's equation and the second identity.
steps.detail: The first step chain gives $\mathbb{E}S_N = \mu\,\mathbb{E}N$ with $S_N$ integrable. The second chain gives $\mathbb{E}(S_N - \mu N)^2 = \sigma^2\,\mathbb{E}N$, which is $\mathbb{E}S_N^2 = \sigma^2\,\mathbb{E}N$ for $\mu = 0$.

concepts.c:iid-random-variables: The steps are i.i.d., so every term has the same mean and variance.
concepts.c:stopping-time: The stopping property puts the event $\{N \ge m\}$ in the past of step $m$.
concepts.c:variance: The variance of one step is the constant in the second identity.
concepts.c:independent-random-variables: Independence of each step from the past splits expectations of products.
concepts.c:filtration: The filtration describes the information that the stopping rule may use.
concepts.c:random-walk: The partial sums $S_n$ form a random walk that is stopped at time $N$.
concepts.c:expected-value: The theorem computes the expected value of the stopped sum.

source.ref: T. S. Ferguson, Optimal Stopping and Applications (UCLA online book), Chapter 3, Section 3.3, Theorem 4 and Proof #1, PDF page 7 of sr3.pdf.
source.note: The first identity follows Proof #1, which exchanges two summations. The second identity is Exercise 4.8.4 in Durrett's Probability: Theory and Examples. These steps prove it with the same series and an L² limit.

statement: If a [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) $X$ indexed by the cube $[0,1]^m$ with values in $\mathbb{R}^d$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}|X_u - X_v|^\beta \le K|u - v|^{m+\alpha}$, then $X$ has a continuous [modification](c:modification) $Y$ that is almost surely [Hölder continuous](c:holder-continuity) with every exponent $\gamma < \alpha/\beta$.

hypotheses.text: $X = (X_u)_{u \in [0,1]^m}$ is a [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) (a random field) indexed by $[0,1]^m$ with values in $\mathbb{R}^d$.
There are constants $\alpha, \beta > 0$ and $K < \infty$ with $\mathbb{E}|X_u - X_v|^\beta \le K|u - v|^{m+\alpha}$ for all $u, v \in [0,1]^m$.

conclusion: There is a field $Y$ with $P(Y_u = X_u) = 1$ for every $u$, continuous paths, and $|Y_u - Y_v| \le C(\omega)|u - v|^\gamma$ almost surely for every $\gamma < \alpha/\beta$.

proofs.name: Dyadic chaining
proofs.slogan: Control all increments at each dyadic level, chain any two [dyadic rationals](c:dyadic-rational-number) through coarser levels, then extend by continuity.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for fields indexed by $[0,1]^m$ with values in $\mathbb{R}^d$.

roles.why: Completeness of $\mathbb{R}^d$ gives the limits that define $Y$ off the dyadic points.
The moment bound makes the level-$n$ failure probabilities summable and gives convergence in probability.

steps.slogan: Bound the chance that some increment between neighbouring points of the dyadic grid of level $n$ exceeds $2^{-\gamma n}$.
steps.detail: Neighbours differ in one coordinate by $2^{-n}$. Markov's inequality and a union bound over at most $m2^{m(n+1)}$ neighbour pairs give $P(G_n^c) \le m2^mK2^{-n(\alpha - \gamma\beta)}$. These are summable, so by Borel-Cantelli almost surely every level $n \ge N(\omega)$ is good.

steps.slogan: Chain two close [dyadic points](c:dyadic-rational-number) through their truncations at levels $\ell, \ell+1, \dots$.
steps.detail: For $2^{-(\ell+1)} \le |r - q| < 2^{-\ell}$ with $\ell \ge N$, the truncations move by at most one grid step in each coordinate per level, so by at most $m$ neighbour steps. Geometric sums give $|X_r - X_q| \le C_\gamma |r - q|^\gamma$ with $C_\gamma = m(2^\gamma + 2/(1 - 2^{-\gamma}))$.

steps.slogan: Join far-apart dyadic points by at most $m2^{N+1}$ short pieces.
steps.detail: Change one coordinate at a time and cut each segment at the points of level $N+1$. Adding the short-range bounds gives $|X_r - X_q| \le m2^{N+1} C_\gamma |r - q|^\gamma$ on all dyadic points.

steps.slogan: Extend the Hölder map from the dense dyadic set to $[0,1]^m$ by [uniform continuity](c:uniform-continuity).
steps.detail: On the intersection of the good events for a sequence $\gamma_j \uparrow \alpha/\beta$, the limit $Y_u = \lim_{q \to u} X_q$ exists and keeps every Hölder bound. Off this event set $Y = 0$.

steps.slogan: Identify $Y_u$ with $X_u$ through [convergence in probability](c:convergence-in-probability).
steps.detail: Markov's inequality gives $X_{q_k} \to X_u$ in probability, and $X_{q_k} \to Y_u$ almost surely. Limits in probability agree almost surely, so $Y$ is a [modification](c:modification) of $X$.

concepts.c:stochastic-process: The theorem upgrades a stochastic process with a moment bound to one with continuous paths.
concepts.c:modification: The continuous process agrees with the given one at each fixed time almost surely.
concepts.c:holder-continuity: The paths of the modification are Hölder continuous with every exponent below alpha over beta.
concepts.c:dyadic-rational-number: The proof controls the field on the countable dense set of points with dyadic rational coordinates first.
concepts.c:uniform-continuity: Uniform continuity on the dyadic points gives a unique continuous extension.
concepts.c:convergence-in-probability: The moment bound gives convergence in probability, which identifies the extension with the process.

source.ref: R. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th edition, Theorem 7.1.3 and Lemma 7.1.4 with their proofs, pp. 357-358.
source.note: Durrett proves the Hölder bound on the dyadic rationals for $m = 1$. The steps extend his chaining to the cube $[0,1]^m$ with neighbour pairs of the grid, and steps s:extend and s:identify add the extension and the modification property.

new_concepts.name: Hölder continuity
new_concepts.reminder: A function is Hölder continuous when its increments are at most a constant times a power of the distance.
new_concepts.definition: A function $f: [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^d$ is Hölder continuous with exponent $\gamma \in (0, 1]$ if there is a constant $C$ with $|f(t) - f(s)| \le C|t - s|^\gamma$ for all $s, t \in [a,b]$. Exponent $1$ gives a [Lipschitz function](c:lipschitz-function), and every Hölder continuous function is [uniformly continuous](c:uniform-continuity).

statement: For a standard [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $B$, almost surely $\limsup_{t\to\infty} B(t)/\sqrt{2t\log\log t} = 1$ and $\liminf_{t\to\infty} B(t)/\sqrt{2t\log\log t} = -1$.

hypotheses.text: $B$ is a standard linear [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion): $B(0) = 0$, the paths are continuous, and $B$ has [independent increments](c:independent-increments) with $B(t) - B(s) \sim N(0, t - s)$.

conclusion: With $\psi(t) = \sqrt{2t\log\log t}$, almost surely $\limsup_{t\to\infty} B(t)/\psi(t) = 1$ and $\liminf_{t\to\infty} B(t)/\psi(t) = -1$.

proofs.name: Geometric blocks and Borel-Cantelli
proofs.slogan: Look at $B$ along the times $q^n$: the first Borel-Cantelli lemma caps the maximum, and independent block increments reach the envelope infinitely often.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem as $t \to \infty$. The local law as $t \downarrow 0$ is not treated.

roles.why: The reflection principle, the scaling of Gaussian tails and the independence of block increments all come from the Brownian structure.

steps.slogan: Bound the [normal distribution](c:normal-distribution) tail above and below by $\varphi(x)/x$.
steps.detail: For $Z \sim N(0,1)$ and $x \ge 1$, integration against $u/x$ and the derivative of $-\varphi(u)/u$ give $\varphi(x)/(2x) \le P(Z > x) \le e^{-x^2/2}$.

steps.slogan: Show that the running maximum exceeds $(1+\varepsilon)\psi(q^n)$ for only finitely many $n$.
steps.detail: The reflection principle gives $P(A_n) = 2P(Z \ge (1+\varepsilon)\sqrt{2\log(n\log q)}) \le 2(n\log q)^{-(1+\varepsilon)^2}$. This is summable, so the [limit superior](c:limsup-of-sets) of the events $A_n$ has probability 0.

steps.slogan: Interpolate between $q^{n-1}$ and $q^n$ to bound the lim sup by $(1+\varepsilon)\sqrt q$.
steps.detail: For $q^{n-1} \le t < q^n$, $B(t)/\psi(t) \le (1+\varepsilon)\psi(q^n)/\psi(q^{n-1}) \to (1+\varepsilon)\sqrt q$. Countably many choices $\varepsilon, q - 1 \downarrow 0$ give $\limsup \le 1$.

steps.slogan: Show that the [independent increments](c:independent-increments) over $(q^{n-1}, q^n]$ reach the envelope infinitely often.
steps.detail: The lower tail bound gives $P(D_n) \ge c/(n\sqrt{\log n})$, which is not summable. The events $D_n$ are independent, so the second Borel-Cantelli lemma makes infinitely many of them occur.

steps.slogan: Combine one large block increment with the upper bound for $-B$ at the previous time.
steps.detail: On $D_n$, $B(q^n) \ge -2\psi(q^{n-1}) + \psi(q^n - q^{n-1})$ for large $n$. Division by $\psi(q^n)$ gives $\limsup \ge \sqrt{1 - 1/q} - 2/\sqrt q$, and $q \to \infty$ gives $\limsup \ge 1$.

steps.slogan: Join the two bounds and apply them to the reflected path $-B$.
steps.detail: The bounds give $\limsup B(t)/\psi(t) = 1$ almost surely. Since $-B$ is a standard [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion), the same holds for $-B$, which gives $\liminf B(t)/\psi(t) = -1$.

concepts.c:brownian-motion: The theorem gives the exact upper envelope of Brownian motion at large times.
concepts.c:independent-increments: Independence of block increments makes the second Borel-Cantelli lemma available.
concepts.c:normal-distribution: Two-sided bounds on the normal tail fix the exact constant in the envelope.
concepts.c:limsup-of-sets: The Borel-Cantelli lemmas decide whether the limit superior of the block events has probability 0 or 1.

source.ref: P. Mörters and Y. Peres, Brownian Motion (Cambridge University Press, 2010), Theorem 5.1 and its proof, pp. 119-120.
source.note: The steps follow the proof in the book. The book cites its Lemma 12.9 for the Gaussian tail bounds, and step s:tails proves them.

statement: For a $d$-dimensional process $X$ whose components are continuous [semimartingales](c:semimartingale) and $F \in C^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$, almost surely for all $t \ge 0$, $F(X_t) = F(X_0) + \sum_i \int_0^t \partial_i F(X_s)\,dX^i_s + \frac12\sum_{i,j}\int_0^t \partial_i\partial_j F(X_s)\,d\langle X^i, X^j\rangle_s$, with [stochastic integrals](c:stochastic-integral) and [quadratic covariations](c:quadratic-variation).

hypotheses.text: Each component $X^i = M^i + A^i$ is a continuous [semimartingale](c:semimartingale): a continuous [local martingale](c:local-martingale) plus a continuous adapted process of [finite variation](c:bounded-variation).
$F\colon \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ is twice continuously differentiable.

conclusion: Almost surely, for all $t \ge 0$, $F(X_t) - F(X_0) = \sum_i \int_0^t \partial_i F(X_s)\,dX^i_s + \frac12\sum_{i,j}\int_0^t \partial_i\partial_j F(X_s)\,d\langle X^i, X^j\rangle_s$.

proofs.name: Second-order Taylor expansion along partitions
proofs.slogan: Expand $F$ to second order along a fine partition, then identify the first-order sum as a stochastic integral and the second-order sum as a bracket integral.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for all times simultaneously.

roles.why: The local martingale part gives the stochastic integral and the bracket, and the finite-variation part gives an ordinary integral.
Continuity of the second derivatives gives the Taylor remainder and makes the remainder error small uniformly.

steps.slogan: Telescope $F(X_t) - F(X_0)$ over a partition and expand each increment to second order.
steps.detail: Taylor's theorem with integral remainder writes each increment as $\nabla F(X_{t_k})\cdot\Delta X_k + \Delta X_k^{T} R_k \Delta X_k$, where $R_k$ averages $\nabla^2 F$ over the segment between $X_{t_k}$ and $X_{t_{k+1}}$. This splits the total change into a first-order sum and a second-order sum.

steps.slogan: Show that left-point Riemann sums converge to the [stochastic integral](c:stochastic-integral).
steps.detail: After stopping, the step integrand differs from the continuous integrand by a bounded amount that tends to 0 uniformly. The isometry and dominated convergence control the martingale part, and the total variation controls the other part. So the first-order sum converges in [probability](c:convergence-in-probability).

steps.slogan: Replace the averaged Hessian by its value at the left endpoint with a vanishing error.
steps.detail: Uniform continuity of $\nabla^2 F$ on a compact set that contains the path makes the largest Hessian error tend to 0 almost surely. The sum of squared increments stays bounded in probability, so Slutsky's theorem kills the product.

steps.slogan: Identify the frozen second-order sum with an integral against the [quadratic covariation](c:quadratic-variation).
steps.detail: Polarization writes the measures of products of increments as differences of measures of squared increments. Along a subsequence their distribution functions converge almost surely on a dense set of times, and Helly-Bray gives convergence of the integrals of the continuous function $\partial_i\partial_j F(X)$.

steps.slogan: Combine the limits in probability and extend from fixed times to all times by continuity.
steps.detail: The exact identity holds for every partition, and the right side converges in probability to the Itô expression. So the formula holds almost surely at each rational time, and continuity of both sides in $t$ gives it for all times at once.

concepts.c:semimartingale: The formula holds for continuous semimartingales and shows that $F(X)$ is again one.
concepts.c:stochastic-integral: The first-order term of the formula is a stochastic integral.
concepts.c:quadratic-variation: The second-order correction integrates against the quadratic covariation of the components.
concepts.c:local-martingale: The local martingale part of $X$ produces the bracket and the stochastic integral.
concepts.c:bounded-variation: The finite-variation part of $X$ contributes an ordinary Stieltjes integral and no bracket.
concepts.c:convergence-in-probability: Riemann sums and quadratic sums converge to their limits in probability.

source.ref: R. Lyons, Stochastic Calculus (lecture notes after Le Gall), Theorem 5.10 with Proposition 5.9 and Lemmas 5A and 5B, pp. 67-70.
source.note: The notes use a mean-value point for the remainder. These steps use the integral form of the remainder and prove the Riemann sum convergence from the isometry.

new_concepts.name: local martingale
new_concepts.reminder: A local martingale becomes a martingale when you stop it at suitable stopping times that increase to infinity.
new_concepts.definition: An adapted [càdlàg](c:is-cadlag) process $(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a local martingale when there are [stopping times](c:stopping-time) $\tau_1\le\tau_2\le\dots$ with $\tau_n\to\infty$ almost surely such that each stopped process $(M_{t\wedge\tau_n}-M_0)_{t\ge0}$ is a [martingale](c:martingale). Such a sequence $(\tau_n)$ is a localizing sequence. A local martingale that is not a martingale is a strict local martingale.

new_concepts.name: quadratic variation
new_concepts.reminder: The quadratic variation of a process is the limit of its sums of squared increments over finer partitions.
new_concepts.definition: For a [semimartingale](c:semimartingale) $X$ and partitions $0=t_0<t_1<\dots<t_k=t$ of $[0,t]$ with mesh tending to $0$, the quadratic variation is $[X]_t=\lim\sum_i(X_{t_{i+1}}-X_{t_i})^2$, where the limit exists in probability. For a continuous [local martingale](c:local-martingale) $M$, $[M]=\langle M\rangle$ is the unique continuous increasing adapted process with $\langle M\rangle_0=0$ such that $M^2-\langle M\rangle$ is a local martingale. A continuous path of finite variation has quadratic variation $0$.

new_concepts.name: semimartingale
new_concepts.reminder: A semimartingale is a local martingale plus an adapted process of finite variation.
new_concepts.definition: An adapted [càdlàg](c:is-cadlag) process $X$ is a semimartingale when $X_t=X_0+M_t+A_t$, where $M$ is a [local martingale](c:local-martingale) with $M_0=0$ and $A$ is an adapted càdlàg process with $A_0=0$ whose paths have [bounded variation](c:bounded-variation) on every bounded interval. The decomposition is not unique in general, but a continuous $X$ has exactly one decomposition with continuous $M$ and $A$. By the Bichteler–Dellacherie theorem, the semimartingales are exactly the good integrators for stochastic integrals.

statement: A continuous adapted process $X$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ is a [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) for its [filtration](c:filtration) if and only if each component is a continuous [local martingale](c:local-martingale) and the [quadratic covariations](c:quadratic-variation) are $\langle X^i, X^j\rangle_t = \delta_{ij} t$.

hypotheses.text: $X = (X^1, \dots, X^d)$ is continuous and adapted to the [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal{F}_t)$.
For the converse direction, each $X^i$ is a continuous [local martingale](c:local-martingale) with $\langle X^i, X^j\rangle_t = \delta_{ij} t$.

conclusion: $X$ is a $d$-dimensional $(\mathcal{F}_t)$-Brownian motion exactly when its components are continuous local martingales with $\langle X^i, X^j\rangle_t = \delta_{ij} t$.

proofs.name: Complex exponential martingale
proofs.slogan: Itô's formula makes $\exp(i\xi\cdot X_t + |\xi|^2 t/2)$ a bounded martingale, which fixes the conditional characteristic function of each increment.
proofs.scope: Both directions. The direct direction is a computation of conditional moments.

roles.why: Adaptedness and continuity are part of the definition of an $(\mathcal{F}_t)$-Brownian motion and are needed for Itô's formula.
The brackets $\delta_{ij} t$ make the drift of the exponential cancel exactly.

steps.slogan: Compute conditional moments of Brownian increments to get the martingale and bracket properties.
steps.detail: With $Y = X - X_0$, [independent increments](c:independent-increments) with mean 0 and covariance $(t-s)I$ make $Y^i$ and $Y^iY^j - \delta_{ij}t$ martingales. Uniqueness of the bracket gives $\langle X^i, X^j\rangle_t = \delta_{ij}t$.

steps.slogan: Show with Itô's formula that the complex exponential of $X$ is a local martingale.
steps.detail: For $Z_t = \exp(i\xi\cdot X_t + |\xi|^2 t/2)$, the time derivative term $\frac{|\xi|^2}{2}Z\,dt$ cancels the bracket term $-\frac12\sum_{j,k}\xi_j\xi_k Z\,d\langle X^j, X^k\rangle$. Only the stochastic integral remains.

steps.slogan: Upgrade the bounded local martingale on $[0,T]$ to a true martingale.
steps.detail: On $[0,T]$ the modulus of $Z$ is at most $e^{|\xi|^2T/2}$. Dominated convergence along a localizing sequence gives $\mathbb{E}[Z_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s] = Z_s$, so $\mathbb{E}[e^{i\xi\cdot(X_t - X_s)}\mid\mathcal{F}_s] = e^{-|\xi|^2(t-s)/2}$.

steps.slogan: Read off independence and the [normal law](c:normal-distribution) from the joint [characteristic function](c:characteristic-function).
steps.detail: For any $\mathcal{F}_s$-measurable vector $W$, the joint characteristic function of $W$ and $X_t - X_s$ factors into that of $W$ times the Gaussian one. Uniqueness of characteristic functions gives independence from $\mathcal{F}_s$ and the law $N(0,(t-s)I)$.

concepts.c:brownian-motion: The theorem characterizes Brownian motion among continuous processes.
concepts.c:filtration: Brownian motion is defined relative to the filtration that the local martingales use.
concepts.c:local-martingale: The components are only assumed to be continuous local martingales.
concepts.c:quadratic-variation: The brackets $\delta_{ij}t$ carry all the information that the theorem needs.
concepts.c:independent-increments: Independence of increments from the past is the conclusion of the converse direction.
concepts.c:normal-distribution: Each increment has the centered normal law with covariance $(t-s)I$.
concepts.c:characteristic-function: The conditional characteristic function of an increment identifies its law and its independence.

new_concepts.name: local martingale
new_concepts.reminder: A local martingale becomes a martingale when you stop it at suitable stopping times that increase to infinity.
new_concepts.definition: An adapted [càdlàg](c:is-cadlag) process $(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a local martingale when there are [stopping times](c:stopping-time) $\tau_1\le\tau_2\le\dots$ with $\tau_n\to\infty$ almost surely such that each stopped process $(M_{t\wedge\tau_n}-M_0)_{t\ge0}$ is a [martingale](c:martingale). Such a sequence $(\tau_n)$ is a localizing sequence. A local martingale that is not a martingale is a strict local martingale.

new_concepts.name: quadratic variation
new_concepts.reminder: The quadratic variation of a process is the limit of its sums of squared increments over finer partitions.
new_concepts.definition: For a [semimartingale](c:semimartingale) $X$ and partitions $0=t_0<t_1<\dots<t_k=t$ of $[0,t]$ with mesh tending to $0$, the quadratic variation is $[X]_t=\lim\sum_i(X_{t_{i+1}}-X_{t_i})^2$, where the limit exists in probability. For a continuous [local martingale](c:local-martingale) $M$, $[M]=\langle M\rangle$ is the unique continuous increasing adapted process with $\langle M\rangle_0=0$ such that $M^2-\langle M\rangle$ is a local martingale. A continuous path of finite variation has quadratic variation $0$.

new_concepts.name: semimartingale
new_concepts.reminder: A semimartingale is a local martingale plus an adapted process of finite variation.
new_concepts.definition: An adapted [càdlàg](c:is-cadlag) process $X$ is a semimartingale when $X_t=X_0+M_t+A_t$, where $M$ is a [local martingale](c:local-martingale) with $M_0=0$ and $A$ is an adapted càdlàg process with $A_0=0$ whose paths have [bounded variation](c:bounded-variation) on every bounded interval. The decomposition is not unique in general, but a continuous $X$ has exactly one decomposition with continuous $M$ and $A$. By the Bichteler–Dellacherie theorem, the semimartingales are exactly the good integrators for stochastic integrals.

statement: For $p > 0$ there are constants $0 < c_p \le C_p$ such that every continuous [local martingale](c:local-martingale) $M$ with $M_0 = 0$ and every [stopping time](c:stopping-time) $T$ satisfy $c_p\,\mathbb{E}\langle M\rangle_T^{p/2} \le \mathbb{E}(M^*_T)^p \le C_p\,\mathbb{E}\langle M\rangle_T^{p/2}$, where $\langle M\rangle$ is the [quadratic variation](c:quadratic-variation).

hypotheses.text: $M$ is a continuous [local martingale](c:local-martingale) with $M_0 = 0$.
$T$ is a [stopping time](c:stopping-time), possibly infinite, and $p > 0$.

conclusion: $c_p\,\mathbb{E}\langle M\rangle_T^{p/2} \le \mathbb{E}\sup_{t \le T}|M_t|^p \le C_p\,\mathbb{E}\langle M\rangle_T^{p/2}$ with $C_p = 2^{p(p+1)/2+p+1}$ and $c_p = 2^{-p^2/4-2p-1}$.

proofs.name: Exit estimate and good-lambda inequalities
proofs.slogan: Bound the chance that one of $M^2$ and $\langle M\rangle$ is large while the other is small, then integrate the tails.
proofs.scope: Both inequalities for every $p > 0$ and every stopping time.

roles.why: Both $M^2 - \langle M\rangle$ and $\langle M\rangle - M^2$ are continuous local martingales, which feeds the exit estimate.
The stopped process $M^T$ is again a continuous local martingale, so the bound at $T = \infty$ gives the general case.

steps.slogan: Bound the probability that a local martingale exits up before it exits down.
steps.detail: The [martingale](c:martingale) stopped at the exit of $(-b, a)$ is bounded and has mean 0, and its limit is $a$ on an up-exit and at least $-b$ otherwise. This gives $P(T_a < T_{-b}) \le \frac{b}{a+b}P(N^*_\infty > 0)$.

steps.slogan: Compare two nonnegative processes whose difference is a local martingale.
steps.detail: If $X$ reaches $\alpha$ while $Y$ stays below $\beta$, then $X - Y$ reaches $\alpha - \beta$ without reaching $-\beta$. The exit estimate bounds this event by $(\beta/\alpha)P((X-Y)^*_\infty > 0)$.

steps.slogan: Derive the two good-lambda inequalities by restarting $M$ at a threshold time.
steps.detail: Restarting $M$ when $|M|$ reaches $\sqrt r$ gives $P((M^*)^2 \ge 4r, \langle M\rangle < br) \le bP((M^*)^2 \ge r)$. Restarting when the [quadratic variation](c:quadratic-variation) reaches $r$ gives $P(\langle M\rangle \ge 2r, (M^*)^2 < br) \le 4bP(\langle M\rangle \ge r)$.

steps.slogan: Integrate the good-lambda bounds against $r^{p/2-1}\,dr$ and absorb the small term.
steps.detail: The tail formula $\mathbb{E}X^q = \kappa^q\int_0^\infty qr^{q-1}P(X \ge \kappa r)\,dr$ turns each tail bound into a moment bound. A small $b$ moves the term $b\,\mathbb{E}(M^*)^p$ or $4b\,\mathbb{E}\langle M\rangle^{p/2}$ to the left side when it is finite.

steps.slogan: Remove the finiteness assumptions by stopping and pass to a general stopping time.
steps.detail: Stopping when $|M|$ or $\langle M\rangle$ reaches $n$ makes the needed moment finite. Monotone convergence as $n \to \infty$ gives both bounds, and applying them to $M^T$ gives them at the [stopping time](c:stopping-time) $T$.

concepts.c:local-martingale: The inequality holds for every continuous local martingale started at 0.
concepts.c:stopping-time: The inequality holds at every stopping time, which also makes localization possible.
concepts.c:quadratic-variation: The quadratic variation is the quantity whose moments are compared with those of the maximum.
concepts.c:martingale: The exit estimate uses the mean-zero property of a bounded stopped martingale.

proofs.name: Interpolation through the exponentials of a scaled martingale
proofs.slogan: Show that $\mathcal{E}(\sqrt{\alpha}M)$ is a martingale for every $\alpha < 1$ by a moment bound, then let $\alpha \to 1$ with Hölder's inequality.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem on a finite horizon.

roles.why: Itô's formula makes $\mathcal{E}(M)$ and $\mathcal{E}(\sqrt{\alpha}M)$ nonnegative local martingales, hence supermartingales.
The finite exponential moment of the bracket bounds $\mathbb{E}\exp(\frac12 M_\sigma)$ uniformly over stopping times.

steps.slogan: Show that nonnegative local martingales are [supermartingales](c:supermartingale), which are martingales when the mean is preserved.
steps.detail: Conditional Fatou along a reducing sequence gives $\mathbb{E}[Z_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s] \le Z_s$. If $\mathbb{E}Z_T = \mathbb{E}Z_0$, the nonnegative gap $Z_s - \mathbb{E}[Z_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s]$ has mean zero and vanishes.

steps.slogan: Bound $\mathbb{E}\exp(\frac12 M_\sigma)$ by $\sqrt{K}$ for every stopping time $\sigma \le T$.
steps.detail: Write $e^{M_\sigma/2} = \mathcal{E}(M)_\sigma^{1/2}e^{\langle M\rangle_\sigma/4}$ and apply Cauchy-Schwarz. The first factor has mean at most 1 by the supermartingale property, and the second has mean at most $K$.

steps.slogan: Show that a uniform $L^u$ bound with $u > 1$ along a reducing sequence gives a martingale.
steps.detail: The stopped values are bounded in $L^u$, hence [uniformly integrable](c:uniform-integrability), and they converge almost surely. Vitali's theorem preserves the mean, and the first step concludes.

steps.slogan: Prove that $\mathcal{E}(\sqrt{\alpha}M)$ is a martingale for each $\alpha < 1$.
steps.detail: Write $\mathcal{E}(\sqrt\alpha M) = \mathcal{E}(M)^\alpha e^{\sqrt\alpha(1-\sqrt\alpha)M}$ and apply Hölder with $u = 1/((2-\sqrt\alpha)\sqrt\alpha) > 1$. This choice turns the exponential factor into $e^{M_\sigma/2}$, whose mean is bounded.

steps.slogan: Let $\alpha$ increase to 1 in a Hölder bound for $\mathbb{E}\,\mathcal{E}(\sqrt{\alpha}M)_T = 1$.
steps.detail: Hölder and Jensen give $1 \le (\mathbb{E}\,\mathcal{E}(M)_T)^\alpha K^{\sqrt\alpha(1-\sqrt\alpha)}$. As $\alpha \to 1$ this forces $\mathbb{E}\,\mathcal{E}(M)_T \ge 1$, and the supermartingale bound gives equality, hence a martingale.

proofs.name: Hölder interpolation through the exponentials of aM
proofs.slogan: Show that $\mathcal{E}(aM)$ is uniformly integrable for $a < 1$, then let $a \to 1$ in a Hölder bound for $\mathbb{E}\,\mathcal{E}(aM)_\infty = 1$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem on $[0,\infty)$.

roles.why: Itô's formula makes every $\mathcal{E}(aM)$ a nonnegative local martingale, hence a [supermartingale](c:supermartingale).
The bound on $\mathbb{E}e^{M_\tau/2}$ controls the exponential factor in every Hölder estimate and makes $M$ bounded above.

steps.slogan: Record that nonnegative local martingales such as $\mathcal{E}(M)$ are supermartingales with mean at most 1.
steps.detail: Itô's formula gives $d\mathcal{E}(L) = \mathcal{E}(L)\,dL$, and conditional Fatou along a reducing sequence gives the [supermartingale](c:supermartingale) property. So $\mathbb{E}\,\mathcal{E}(M)_\tau \le 1$ for bounded $\tau$.

steps.slogan: Show that $M$ is bounded above and converges, with $\mathbb{E}e^{M_\infty/2} \le K$.
steps.detail: At the hitting time of level $n$, $e^{n/2}P(\rho_n < \infty) \le K$, so $M$ is bounded above almost surely. Below a level, $n - M$ is a nonnegative supermartingale and converges. Fatou gives $\mathbb{E}e^{M_\infty/2} \le K$.

steps.slogan: Prove that $\mathcal{E}(aM)$ is a uniformly integrable martingale for each $a < 1$.
steps.detail: Write $\mathcal{E}(aM) = \mathcal{E}(M)^{a^2}(e^{cM})^{1-a^2}$ with $c = a/(1+a) < \frac12$. Two Hölder steps give $\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{E}(aM)_\tau 1_A] \le P(A)^{(1-a)^2}K^{2a(1-a)}$, which is uniform integrability over bounded $\tau$. Vitali's theorem then gives the martingale property and $\mathbb{E}\,\mathcal{E}(aM)_\infty = 1$.

steps.slogan: Let $a$ increase to 1 in the Hölder bound at time infinity.
steps.detail: Hölder and Jensen give $1 \le (\mathbb{E}\,\mathcal{E}(M)_\infty)^{a^2}K^{2a(1-a)}$. As $a \to 1$ the factor with $K$ tends to 1, so $\mathbb{E}\,\mathcal{E}(M)_\infty \ge 1$.

steps.slogan: Close the supermartingale $\mathcal{E}(M)$ by its limit to get a uniformly integrable martingale.
steps.detail: Fatou gives $\mathbb{E}\,\mathcal{E}(M)_\infty \le 1$, so the mean is exactly 1. The nonnegative gap $\mathcal{E}(M)_t - \mathbb{E}[\mathcal{E}(M)_\infty\mid\mathcal{F}_t]$ has mean at most 0 and vanishes.

The [quadratic variation](c:quadratic-variation) satisfies $\langle M\rangle_\infty = \infty$ almost surely.

conclusion: $\beta_r = M_{\tau_r}$ is a Brownian motion for the filtration $(\mathcal{F}_{\tau_r})$, and almost surely $M_t = \beta_{\langle M\rangle_t}$ for all $t \ge 0$.

proofs.name: Inverse clock and Lévy's characterization
proofs.slogan: Run $M$ on the inverse of its own clock $\langle M\rangle$, check that the result is continuous, and recognize a Brownian motion by its martingale properties.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with any initial value $M_0$.

roles.why: The bracket of $M$ exists, and stopped versions of $M$ and $M^2 - \langle M\rangle$ are uniformly integrable martingales.
Every level $r$ of the clock is reached, so the [stopping times](c:stopping-time) $\tau_r$ are finite and $\beta$ is defined for all $r$.

steps.slogan: Show that $M$ stays constant on every interval where its bracket is constant.
steps.detail: For $N_t = M_t - M_{t\wedge a}$, Doob's inequality gives $\mathbb{E}\sup_t N_{t\wedge S^\varepsilon}^2 \le 4\varepsilon$ when $S^\varepsilon$ stops $N$ once its bracket reaches $\varepsilon$. Letting $\varepsilon \to 0$ shows that $N = 0$ until its bracket leaves 0. Rational $a$ and continuity cover all intervals.

steps.slogan: Prove that the time-changed process $\beta_r = M_{\tau_r}$ is continuous and recovers $M$.
steps.detail: The inverse clock $\tau_r$ jumps only across intervals where $\langle M\rangle$ is flat, and $M$ is constant on those intervals. So $\beta$ has no jumps, and $\tau_{\langle M\rangle_t} \le t \le \tau_{\langle M\rangle_t +}$ gives $M_t = \beta_{\langle M\rangle_t}$.

steps.slogan: Transfer the [martingale](c:martingale) properties of $M$ and $M^2 - \langle M\rangle$ to $\beta$ by optional stopping.
steps.detail: Stopped at $\tau_n$, both processes are [uniformly integrable](c:uniform-integrability) martingales because the bracket is at most $n$. Optional stopping at $\tau_r \le \tau_s$ shows that $\beta - \beta_0$ and $(\beta - \beta_0)^2 - r$ are martingales for $\mathcal{F}_{\tau_r}$.

steps.slogan: Identify $\beta$ as a Brownian motion with Lévy's characterization.
steps.detail: The process $\beta$ is a continuous local martingale for the time-changed filtration with bracket $\langle\beta\rangle_r = r$. Lévy's characterization then gives independent Gaussian increments with variance $s - r$.

concepts.c:brownian-motion: The time-changed process is a Brownian motion.
concepts.c:quadratic-variation: The quadratic variation is the random clock that the time change inverts.
concepts.c:filtration: The Brownian motion is adapted to the time-changed filtration of the stopping times.
concepts.c:stopping-time: The inverse clock consists of stopping times, so optional stopping applies.
concepts.c:martingale: The martingale properties of $M$ and $M^2 - \langle M\rangle$ pass to $\beta$.

new_concepts.name: quadratic variation

statement: For [continuous local martingales](c:local-martingale) $M$ and $N$ and measurable processes $H$ and $K$, almost surely $\int_0^\infty |H_s||K_s|\,|d\langle M,N\rangle_s| \le \left(\int_0^\infty H_s^2\,d\langle M\rangle_s\right)^{1/2}\left(\int_0^\infty K_s^2\,d\langle N\rangle_s\right)^{1/2}$, where the brackets are [quadratic variation](c:quadratic-variation) processes.

hypotheses.text: $M$ and $N$ are continuous [local martingales](c:local-martingale) for the same [filtration](c:filtration).
$H$ and $K$ are jointly measurable in $(t,\omega)$, so each path is a Borel function of $t$.

proofs.name: Quadratic discriminant and monotone class
proofs.slogan: Bound the bracket increments on intervals by a discriminant, extend the bound to all Borel sets, then to all functions.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, including the bound for the signed integral.

roles.why: The brackets exist, are continuous and bilinear, and $\langle M+\lambda N\rangle$ is nondecreasing.
Each path of $H$ and $K$ is a Borel function, so the deterministic bound applies path by path.

steps.slogan: Bound each bracket increment by a discriminant of a nonnegative quadratic.
steps.detail: The increment of $\langle M+\lambda N\rangle$ over $(s,t]$ equals $\Delta\langle M\rangle + 2\lambda\Delta\langle M,N\rangle + \lambda^2\Delta\langle N\rangle \ge 0$. A null set that serves all rational $\lambda, s, t$ and continuity give $(\Delta\langle M,N\rangle)^2 \le \Delta\langle M\rangle\,\Delta\langle N\rangle$ for all $s<t$.

steps.slogan: Extend the interval bound to every Borel set by the monotone class theorem.
steps.detail: For finite unions of intervals the bound $|\mu_a(B)| \le (v_1(B)v_2(B))^{1/2}$ follows from Cauchy-Schwarz for sums. The good sets form a monotone class that contains an algebra, so they contain all Borel sets. Summing over partitions gives the same bound for the [total variation](c:bounded-variation) measure of the [signed measure](c:signed-measure) $\mu_a$.

steps.slogan: Pass from indicators to nonnegative Borel functions with simple functions and monotone limits.
steps.detail: For simple $h$ and $k$ on a common partition, Cauchy-Schwarz for sums gives $\int hk\,d|\mu_a| \le (\int h^2dv_1)^{1/2}(\int k^2dv_2)^{1/2}$. Monotone convergence extends this to nonnegative Borel $h$ and $k$ and then from $(0,T]$ to $(0,\infty)$.

steps.slogan: Apply the deterministic bound to the paths of $H$ and $K$ for each good outcome.
steps.detail: Outside the null set of the first step, the paths $|H(\omega)|$ and $|K(\omega)|$ are nonnegative Borel functions, so the function bound applies to them. The signed integral is at most the integral against the total variation measure.

concepts.c:quadratic-variation: The brackets $\langle M\rangle$ and $\langle N\rangle$ are the quadratic variations that weight the right side.
concepts.c:filtration: Both local martingales are adapted to one common filtration, so their bracket exists.
concepts.c:bounded-variation: The cross bracket has finite variation, so it defines a total variation measure.
concepts.c:signed-measure: The cross bracket defines a signed measure whose total variation the proof bounds.

hypotheses.text: $M$ is a continuous [martingale](c:martingale) with $M_0 = 0$ and $\sup_t \mathbb{E} M_t^2 < \infty$, for a [filtration](c:filtration) with the usual conditions.

proofs.name: Isometry on step processes and extension by density
proofs.slogan: Compute the second moment for step integrands, show that step integrands are dense, and extend into the complete space of martingales.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem.

roles.why: Boundedness in $L^2$ makes $\mathbb{H}^2$ a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) and makes $M^2 - \langle M\rangle$ a true martingale.
The integrand lies in $L^2(M)$, the space on which the extension is defined.

steps.slogan: Show that continuous $L^2$-bounded martingales form a complete space.
steps.detail: A Cauchy sequence has terminal values that converge in $L^2$ to some $Z$. Doob's inequality gives a subsequence that converges uniformly in time almost surely, and the limit equals $\mathbb{E}[Z\mid\mathcal{F}_t]$, a continuous martingale bounded in $L^2$. So $\mathbb{H}^2$ is a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space).

steps.slogan: Compute the second moment of the integral of a step process by conditioning.
steps.detail: Cross terms vanish because each later increment of $M$ has conditional mean zero. Each diagonal term gives $\mathbb{E}[H_{(i)}^2(\langle M\rangle_{t_{i+1}} - \langle M\rangle_{t_i})]$ because $M^2 - \langle M\rangle$ is a true martingale. The sum is $\mathbb{E}\int H^2\,d\langle M\rangle$.

steps.slogan: Prove that step processes are [dense](c:dense-set) by showing their orthogonal complement is zero.
steps.detail: If $K$ is orthogonal to all step processes, then $X_t = \int_0^t K\,d\langle M\rangle$ is a continuous martingale of integrable variation. Such a martingale is zero, because its squared increments sum to at most its variation times the largest increment. So $K = 0$ in $L^2(M)$.

steps.slogan: Extend the isometry from step processes to all of $L^2(M)$ by uniform continuity.
steps.detail: Approximate $H$ by step processes. Their integrals form a Cauchy sequence in the complete space $\mathbb{H}^2$, the limit does not depend on the sequence, and the norm identity passes to the limit. Uniqueness holds because the step processes are dense.

concepts.c:martingale: The integrator is a continuous martingale bounded in $L^2$, and so is the integral.
concepts.c:stochastic-integral: The theorem constructs the stochastic integral as the extension of an isometry.
concepts.c:isometry: The integral map preserves the $L^2$ norm, which makes the extension unique.
concepts.c:filtration: The integrand and the integrator are adapted to one filtration with the usual conditions.
concepts.c:quadratic-variation: The quadratic variation of $M$ is the measure that defines the norm of $L^2(M)$.
concepts.c:hilbert-space: Completeness of $\mathbb{H}^2$ gives the limit of the approximating integrals.
concepts.c:dense-set: Density of step processes lets one isometry extend to all integrands.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a continuous [semimartingale](c:semimartingale) with $X_0 = 0$ and [quadratic variation](c:quadratic-variation) $\langle X\rangle$.

proofs.name: Itô's formula for the candidate and for its inverse
proofs.slogan: Itô's formula shows that $e^{X - \langle X\rangle/2}$ solves the equation, and the product with its inverse shows that no other solution exists.
proofs.scope: The continuous case.

roles.why: Itô's formula needs a continuous semimartingale, and the [quadratic variation](c:quadratic-variation) of $X$ gives the second-order term that the $-\frac12\langle X\rangle$ cancels.

steps.slogan: Apply Itô's formula to $F(x,v) = e^{x - v/2}$ at $(X, \langle X\rangle)$.
steps.detail: The $dv$ term $-\frac12 Z\,d\langle X\rangle$ cancels the second-order term $+\frac12 Z\,d\langle X\rangle$, so $dZ = Z\,dX$ and $Z_0 = 1$.

steps.slogan: A stochastic integral against a local martingale is a local martingale.
steps.detail: If $X$ is a continuous [local martingale](c:local-martingale), then $Z = 1 + \int Z\,dX$ is a [stochastic integral](c:stochastic-integral) of a continuous adapted process, so it is a local martingale by localization.

steps.slogan: Compute the differential of the inverse $U = 1/Z$ with Itô's formula.
steps.detail: With $G(x,v) = e^{-x + v/2}$ Itô's formula gives $dU = -U\,dX + U\,d\langle X\rangle$, a drift term that will cancel the covariation.

steps.slogan: Show that the product of any solution $Y$ with $U$ is constant.
steps.detail: The product rule gives $d(YU) = Y\,dU + U\,dY + d\langle Y,U\rangle$, and $d\langle Y,U\rangle = -YU\,d\langle X\rangle$. All four terms cancel, so $YU \equiv 1$.

steps.slogan: Conclude existence, uniqueness and the local martingale property.
steps.detail: From $YU \equiv 1$ we get $Y = 1/U = Z$ for all times almost surely, so the solution is unique and equals the [stochastic exponential](c:stochastic-exponential).

concepts.c:local-martingale: The solution is a local martingale when the driver is a local martingale.

proofs.name: Itô's formula for a C¹ rounding of the absolute value
proofs.slogan: Round off the corner of $|y - a|$ at scale $\varepsilon$, apply Itô's formula, and let $\varepsilon \to 0$ with Doob's inequality and the isometry.
proofs.scope: The whole statement for a fixed level $a$.

roles.why: Brownian motion has normal marginals, so it spends zero [Lebesgue](c:lebesgue-measure) time at each level, and its [Itô integrals](c:ito-integral) satisfy the isometry with $d\langle B\rangle_s = ds$.

steps.slogan: Brownian motion spends zero Lebesgue time at any fixed level.
steps.detail: By Fubini, $\mathbb{E}\,\mathrm{Leb}\{s \le T : B_s = c\} = \int_0^T P(B_s = c)\,ds = 0$, because $B_s$ has a density for $s > 0$.

steps.slogan: Replace the corner of $|y - a|$ by a parabola on $(a - \varepsilon, a + \varepsilon)$.
steps.detail: The function $f_\varepsilon$ is $C^1$, within $\varepsilon/2$ of $|y - a|$, its derivative differs from $\operatorname{sgn}(y - a)$ only near $a$, and its second derivative is $\frac1\varepsilon 1\{|y - a| < \varepsilon\}$.

steps.slogan: Itô's formula for $f_\varepsilon$ produces the occupation time near $a$.
steps.detail: Mollify $f_\varepsilon$, apply Itô's formula, and pass to the limit with Doob's inequality and dominated convergence. The second-order term becomes $\frac{1}{2\varepsilon}\int_0^t 1\{|B_s - a| < \varepsilon\}\,ds$.

steps.slogan: Let $\varepsilon \to 0$: the error integral is controlled by the time spent near $a$.
steps.detail: Doob and the isometry bound $\mathbb{E}\sup_{t\le T}|L^{a,\varepsilon}_t - L^a_t|^2$ by $2\varepsilon^2 + 8\,\mathbb{E}\int_0^T 1\{|B_s - a| < \varepsilon\}\,ds$, which tends to 0 by the zero-time step.

steps.slogan: Pass monotonicity and support to the [local time](c:local-time) along an almost surely convergent subsequence.
steps.detail: Borel–Cantelli gives $\varepsilon_k$ with uniform convergence on compacts almost surely. Each approximation is nondecreasing and constant on intervals where $B$ stays away from $a$, and the limit keeps both properties.

new_concepts.name: local time
new_concepts.reminder: The local time $L_t^x$ measures how much time a process spends near the level $x$ up to time $t$.
new_concepts.definition: For a one-dimensional [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $B$, the local time is the jointly continuous process $(L_t^x)_{t\ge0,x\in\mathbb{R}}$ such that $\int_0^tf(B_s)\,ds=\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x)L_t^x\,dx$ for all bounded Borel functions $f$ and all $t$, almost surely. So $x\mapsto L_t^x$ is the [Radon–Nikodym derivative](c:radon-nikodym-derivative) of the occupation measure $A\mapsto\int_0^t1_A(B_s)\,ds$ with respect to [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure). For a continuous [semimartingale](c:semimartingale) $X$, the same formula with $d\langle X\rangle_s$ in place of $ds$ defines $L_t^x$, which is then right-continuous in $x$.

statement: For a [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $B$ from $0$ there is a continuous field $L(t,x) \ge 0$ of [local times](c:local-time) such that, almost surely, $\int_0^t f(B_s)\,ds = \int_{\mathbb{R}} f(x)\,L(t,x)\,dx$ for all $t \ge 0$ and every bounded [measurable](c:measurable-function) $f$.

hypotheses.text: $B$ is a standard linear [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) with $B_0 = 0$.
The test function $f$ is bounded and [measurable](c:measurable-function).

conclusion: Almost surely, $L(t,\cdot)$ is the density of the occupation measure $A \mapsto \int_0^t 1_A(B_s)\,ds$ with respect to [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) for every $t \ge 0$, and $L(\cdot,x)$ is the Tanaka local time at $x$.

proofs.name: Moment bound, continuous version and comparison with Itô's formula
proofs.slogan: Make the Tanaka integrals continuous in the level by a moment bound, then compare Tanaka's and Itô's formulas against a test function.
proofs.scope: The full statement for Brownian motion from 0.

roles.why: Gaussian transition densities bound the occupation moments, and Itô calculus for $B$ gives the two formulas that the proof compares.
A bounded measurable $f$ is a uniform limit of simple functions, so the identity for Borel sets gives the identity for $f$.

steps.slogan: Bound the sixth moment of the increments of the Tanaka integral field $I(t,x)$.
steps.detail: For $I(t,x) = \int_0^t 1\{B_s \le x\}\,dB_s$ the Burkholder–Davis–Gundy inequality reduces the sixth moment to the third moment of an occupation time. Gaussian densities bound that by $6(y-x)^3(2T/\pi)^{3/2}$, so $E|I(t,y)-I(u,x)|^6 \le C(|t-u|+|y-x|)^3$.

steps.slogan: Build a jointly continuous version of $I$ and define $L$ from Tanaka's formula.
steps.detail: After an affine change of each rectangle $[0,T] \times [-T,T]$ to $[0,1]^2$, the exponent $3 = m + 1$ with $m = 2$ fits the Kolmogorov–Chentsov theorem for fields on $[0,1]^2$, which gives a continuous [modification](c:modification) $\tilde I$. Then $L(t,x) = 2[(B_t-x)^+ - (-x)^+ - B_t + \tilde I(t,x)]$ is continuous and satisfies Tanaka's formula at each level.

steps.slogan: Expand $F(B_t)$ with Itô's formula for a primitive $F$ of a test function $h$.
steps.detail: For continuous $h$ with [compact support](c:compact-support) put $F(z) = \int h(y)(z-y)^+\,dy$. Then $F'' = h$ and $F' = c - G$ with $G(z) = \int h(y)1\{z \le y\}\,dy$, so $F(B_t)-F(0) = cB_t - \int_0^t G(B_s)\,dB_s + \frac12\int_0^t h(B_s)\,ds$.

steps.slogan: Exchange the [Itô integral](c:ito-integral) and the integral over levels with Riemann sums.
steps.detail: The step functions $G_m(z) = \sum_k h(y_k)\Delta\,1\{z \le y_k\}$ converge uniformly to $G$. Their stochastic integrals are [Riemann sums](c:riemann-sum) $\sum_k h(y_k)\Delta\,\tilde I(t,y_k)$. The Itô isometry and continuity of $\tilde I$ give $\int_0^t G(B_s)\,dB_s = \int h(y)\tilde I(t,y)\,dy$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two expansions into the occupation identity for continuous test functions.
steps.detail: Writing $F(B_t)-F(0)$ and $cB_t$ as integrals of $h$ against $(B_t-y)^+ - (-y)^+$ and $B_t$, the Itô expansion becomes $\frac12\int_0^t h(B_s)\,ds = \frac12\int h(y)L(t,y)\,dy$ almost surely.

steps.slogan: Extend the identity to all times, all Borel sets and all bounded measurable functions.
steps.detail: Continuous $h_j \uparrow 1_{(a,b)}$ give the identity for rational intervals and rational times on one full event. Continuity gives $L \ge 0$ and all times. Dynkin's $\pi$-$\lambda$ theorem gives all Borel sets, and simple functions give every bounded measurable $f$.

concepts.c:local-time: The local times at all levels form the density of the occupation measure.
concepts.c:measurable-function: The formula holds for every bounded measurable test function at once.
concepts.c:lebesgue-measure: The local time is a density with respect to Lebesgue measure on the line.
concepts.c:modification: A continuous modification of the Tanaka integrals gives a local time field that is continuous in both variables.
concepts.c:compact-support: Compact support of the test function keeps the level integrals over a bounded interval.
concepts.c:ito-integral: The Tanaka integral at each level is an Itô integral against the Brownian motion.

So $x\mapsto L_t^x$ is the [Radon–Nikodym derivative](c:radon-nikodym-derivative) of the occupation measure $A\mapsto\int_0^t1_A(B_s)\,ds$ with respect to [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure).
