statement: For a standard [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $B$ with running maximum $M$ and [local time](c:local-time) $L$ at $0$, the [processes](c:stochastic-process) $(M - B, M)$ and $(|B|, L)$ have the same [joint distribution](c:joint-distribution).

hypotheses.text: $B$ is a standard linear [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) with $B(0) = 0$.

$L$ is the [local time](c:local-time) of $B$ at $0$ in Tanaka's formula $|B(t)| = \int_0^t \operatorname{sign}(B(s))\,dB(s) + L(t)$, with $L(t) = \lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow 0}(2\varepsilon)^{-1}\,\mathrm{Leb}\{s \le t : |B(s)| \le \varepsilon\}$.

conclusion: $((M(t) - B(t), M(t)))_{t\ge 0}$ and $((|B(t)|, L(t)))_{t\ge 0}$ have the same law on $C([0,\infty), \mathbb{R}^2)$.

proofs.name: Tanaka's formula and the reflection argument
proofs.slogan: Tanaka's formula writes $|B| = L - \tilde W$ for a Brownian motion $\tilde W$, and $L$ is exactly the running maximum of $\tilde W$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem.

roles.why: Brownian motion makes $W = \int \operatorname{sign}(B)\,dB$ a continuous martingale with quadratic variation $t$, and the law of $\Phi(B)$ is the target law.
Tanaka's formula links $L$ to $|B|$, and the occupation density shows that $L$ grows only on the zero set.

steps.slogan: Write $|B| = W + L$ with Tanaka's formula, where $W$ is a stochastic integral.
steps.detail: Tanaka's formula at level $0$ gives $|B(t)| = W(t) + L(t)$ for all $t$, where $W(t) = \int_0^t \operatorname{sign}(B(s))\,dB(s)$ is an [Itô integral](c:ito-integral) of a bounded adapted integrand.

steps.slogan: Show that $W$ is a Brownian motion through its quadratic variation and Lévy's characterization.
steps.detail: The [quadratic variation](c:quadratic-variation) is $\langle W\rangle_t = t - \mathrm{Leb}\{s \le t : B(s) = 0\}$, and Tonelli's theorem shows that the zero set has [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) $0$. So $\langle W\rangle_t = t$, and $W$ and $\tilde W = -W$ are standard Brownian motions.

steps.slogan: Show that the local time is nondecreasing and grows only on the zero set of $B$.
steps.detail: For rational $s < t$ the increment $L(t) - L(s)$ is the limit of $(2\varepsilon)^{-1}$ times the time spent in $[-\varepsilon, \varepsilon]$ during $[s,t]$. It is nonnegative, and it is zero when $B$ has no zero on $[s,t]$. Continuity extends this to all intervals.

steps.slogan: Identify $L$ with the running maximum of $\tilde W$ by a two-sided comparison.
steps.detail: From $\tilde W = L - |B| \le L$ we get $\max_{s \le t}\tilde W(s) \le L(t)$. At the last zero $s^*$ of $B$ before $t$, $L(t) = L(s^*) = \tilde W(s^*) \le \max_{s\le t}\tilde W(s)$. So $L = \tilde M$ and $|B| = \tilde M - \tilde W$ pathwise.

steps.slogan: Transfer the pathwise identity to an identity in law with a continuous path map.
steps.detail: The map $\Phi(w) = (\max w - w, \max w)$ is continuous on path space. Since $(|B|, L) = \Phi(\tilde W)$ and $\tilde W$ has the law of $B$, the pair has the law of $\Phi(B) = (M - B, M)$.

concepts.c:joint-distribution: The two coordinates are compared jointly, as one two-dimensional law.
concepts.c:ito-integral: The process W is the Itô integral of sign(B) against B.

new_concepts.name: local martingale
new_concepts.reminder: A local martingale becomes a martingale when you stop it at suitable stopping times that increase to infinity.
new_concepts.definition: An adapted [càdlàg](c:is-cadlag) process $(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a local martingale when there are [stopping times](c:stopping-time) $\tau_1\le\tau_2\le\dots$ with $\tau_n\to\infty$ almost surely such that each stopped process $(M_{t\wedge\tau_n}-M_0)_{t\ge0}$ is a [martingale](c:martingale). Such a sequence $(\tau_n)$ is a localizing sequence. A local martingale that is not a martingale is a strict local martingale.

new_concepts.name: local time
new_concepts.reminder: The local time $L_t^x$ measures how much time a process spends near the level $x$ up to time $t$.
new_concepts.definition: For a one-dimensional [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $B$, the local time is the jointly continuous process $(L_t^x)_{t\ge0,x\in\mathbb{R}}$ such that $\int_0^tf(B_s)\,ds=\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x)L_t^x\,dx$ for all bounded Borel functions $f$ and all $t$, almost surely. So $x\mapsto L_t^x$ is the [Radon–Nikodym derivative](c:radon-nikodym-derivative) of the occupation measure $A\mapsto\int_0^t1_A(B_s)\,ds$ with respect to [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure). For a continuous [semimartingale](c:semimartingale) $X$, the same formula with $d\langle X\rangle_s$ in place of $ds$ defines $L_t^x$, which is then right-continuous in $x$.

new_concepts.name: quadratic variation
new_concepts.reminder: The quadratic variation of a process is the limit of its sums of squared increments over finer partitions.
new_concepts.definition: For a [semimartingale](c:semimartingale) $X$ and partitions $0=t_0<t_1<\dots<t_k=t$ of $[0,t]$ with mesh tending to $0$, the quadratic variation is $[X]_t=\lim\sum_i(X_{t_{i+1}}-X_{t_i})^2$, where the limit exists in probability. For a continuous [local martingale](c:local-martingale) $M$, $[M]=\langle M\rangle$ is the unique continuous increasing adapted process with $\langle M\rangle_0=0$ such that $M^2-\langle M\rangle$ is a local martingale. A continuous path of finite variation has quadratic variation $0$.

new_concepts.name: semimartingale
new_concepts.reminder: A semimartingale is a local martingale plus an adapted process of finite variation.
new_concepts.definition: An adapted [càdlàg](c:is-cadlag) process $X$ is a semimartingale when $X_t=X_0+M_t+A_t$, where $M$ is a [local martingale](c:local-martingale) with $M_0=0$ and $A$ is an adapted càdlàg process with $A_0=0$ whose paths have [bounded variation](c:bounded-variation) on every bounded interval. The decomposition is not unique in general, but a continuous $X$ has exactly one decomposition with continuous $M$ and $A$. By the Bichteler–Dellacherie theorem, the semimartingales are exactly the good integrators for stochastic integrals.

statement: For a [stochastic differential equation](c:stochastic-differential-equation) with continuous coefficients and a weak solution, [pathwise uniqueness](c:pathwise-uniqueness) holds if and only if the [joint distribution](c:joint-distribution) of the solution and the [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) is unique and a [strong solution](c:strong-solution) exists.

hypotheses.text: The drift $b(t,x)$ and the diffusion matrix $\sigma(t,x)$ are continuous.
Some filtered probability space carries a [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $W$ and a continuous adapted solution $X$ with $X_0$ of law $\mu$.

conclusion: Pathwise uniqueness is equivalent to uniqueness of the law of $(X, W)$ together with $X = F(X_0, W)$ for a Borel map $F$. Then every solution is $F(X_0, W)$ and is adapted to the filtration of $(X_0, W)$.

proofs.name: Randomized solutions coupled on one space
proofs.slogan: Write each solution law as a function of the noise and an independent uniform variable, put two of them on one space, and let pathwise uniqueness merge them.
proofs.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 3.14 in Kurtz (2007), pp. 959-960, for stochastic differential equations as in Example 3.9.

roles.why: Continuous coefficients make the integrals limits of Riemann sums, so being a solution is a condition on the joint law of $(X, X_0, W)$.
A weak solution gives a solution law to randomize, so the set of solution laws is not empty.

steps.slogan: Recast a solution as a joint law of $(X, Y)$ with $Y = (X_0, W)$ and a compatibility condition.
steps.detail: The equation becomes limit conditions on the [joint distribution](c:joint-distribution) of $(X, Y)$, and compatibility means that $W(t+\cdot)-W(t)$ is independent of the past of $(X, W)$. The set of solution laws is convex (Lemmas 3.2 and 3.8 of the source).

steps.slogan: Represent a solution law as $(F(Y,\xi), Y)$ with an independent uniform variable $\xi$.
steps.detail: Disintegration gives a [Markov kernel](c:markov-kernel) $\eta(y,dx)$ with $\hat\mu(dx\,dy) = \eta(y,dx)\nu(dy)$, and a Borel sampling map $H$ turns a [uniform](c:uniform-distribution) $\xi$ into a variable of law $\eta(y,\cdot)$ (Lemmas 2.2 and A.1).

steps.slogan: Put two randomized solutions on one space with the same noise and prove joint compatibility.
steps.detail: With $Y, \xi_1, \xi_2$ independent, $X_1 = F_{\hat\mu}(Y,\xi_1)$ and $X_2 = F_{\hat\gamma}(Y,\xi_2)$ satisfy $E[f(Y) \mid \mathcal F_t^{X_1} \vee \mathcal F_t^{X_2} \vee \mathcal F_t^Y] = E[f(Y) \mid \mathcal F_t^Y]$ by Lemma 3.7 and a chain of [conditional expectations](c:conditional-expectation).

steps.slogan: Pathwise uniqueness merges the two solutions, which gives one law and a strong solution.
steps.detail: From $X_1 = X_2$ almost surely the two laws agree. Lemma A.2 shows that a function of $(Y, \xi_1)$ that equals a function of $(Y, \xi_2)$ is a function $F(Y)$ of $Y$ alone.

steps.slogan: Show that the [strong solution](c:strong-solution) $F(X_0, W)$ is adapted and solves the equation on every space.
steps.detail: Lemma 3.11 gives $g(X) = E[g(F(Y)) \mid \mathcal F_t^Y]$ for $g$ measurable in the path up to time $t$. So $F(X_0, W)$ is adapted to the noise, and its law is the solution law on any space.

steps.slogan: Derive pathwise uniqueness from a unique law that a strong solution carries.
steps.detail: If the only solution law is the law of $(F(Y), Y)$, its kernel is $\delta_{F(y)}$, so two solutions with the same $Y$ both equal $F(Y)$ almost surely. This gives [pathwise uniqueness](c:pathwise-uniqueness).

concepts.c:pathwise-uniqueness: Pathwise uniqueness is one side of the equivalence and merges two coupled solutions.
concepts.c:joint-distribution: Uniqueness in law here means uniqueness of the joint law of the solution and the noise.
concepts.c:brownian-motion: The Brownian motion is the noise of which the strong solution is a functional.
concepts.c:strong-solution: A strong solution is a Borel functional of the initial value and the noise.
concepts.c:markov-kernel: The conditional law of the solution given the noise is a Markov kernel from the noise space.
concepts.c:uniform-distribution: An independent uniform variable carries the extra randomness of a weak solution.

new_concepts.name: pathwise uniqueness
new_concepts.reminder: Pathwise uniqueness means that two solutions driven by the same Brownian motion from the same start agree almost surely.
new_concepts.definition: A [stochastic differential equation](c:stochastic-differential-equation) $dX_t=b(t,X_t)\,dt+\sigma(t,X_t)\,dB_t$ has pathwise uniqueness when, for any two solutions $X$ and $X'$ on a common filtered probability space with the same [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $B$ and $X_0=X'_0$ almost surely, $P(X_t=X'_t\text{ for all }t\ge0)=1$. By the Yamada–Watanabe theorem, weak existence and pathwise uniqueness together give a unique [strong solution](c:strong-solution) and uniqueness in law.

new_concepts.name: strong solution of a stochastic differential equation
new_concepts.reminder: A strong solution of a stochastic differential equation is built from the given Brownian motion and initial value alone.
new_concepts.definition: Fix a probability space with a [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $B$, an initial value $\xi$ independent of $B$, and the [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal{F}_t)$ that $\xi$ and $B$ generate, augmented by the null sets. A strong solution of the [stochastic differential equation](c:stochastic-differential-equation) $dX_t=b(t,X_t)\,dt+\sigma(t,X_t)\,dB_t$ with $X_0=\xi$ is a continuous process $X$ adapted to $(\mathcal{F}_t)$ such that both integrals exist and $X_t=\xi+\int_0^tb(s,X_s)\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma(s,X_s)\,dB_s$ for all $t$, almost surely. A weak solution, in contrast, can use a Brownian motion and a filtration that are constructed together with $X$.

statement: For a one-dimensional [stochastic differential equation](c:stochastic-differential-equation) with a [Lipschitz](c:lipschitz-continuous-function) drift and a diffusion coefficient with modulus $\rho$ such that $\int_0^\gamma \rho(u)^{-2}\,du = \infty$, [pathwise uniqueness](c:pathwise-uniqueness) holds.

hypotheses.text: The drift satisfies $|b(t,x)-b(t,y)| \le K|x-y|$ for $|x-y| \le \gamma$; it is [Lipschitz](c:lipschitz-continuous-function) at small distances.

The diffusion coefficient satisfies $|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)| \le \rho(|x-y|)$ for $|x-y| \le \gamma$, with $\rho$ nondecreasing, positive on $(0,\gamma]$ and $\int_0^\gamma \rho(u)^{-2}\,du = \infty$.
$X$ and $Y$ solve the equation on one probability space with the same [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $W$ and $X_0 = Y_0$ almost surely.

conclusion: $X$ and $Y$ are indistinguishable: almost surely $X_t = Y_t$ for all $t \ge 0$.

proofs.name: Smoothed absolute value and Grönwall's lemma
proofs.slogan: Apply Itô's formula to smooth approximations of $|X-Y|$ whose second derivative is at most $2/(k\rho^2)$, so the noise term costs only $1/k$.
proofs.scope: The full one-dimensional statement.

roles.why: The Lipschitz bound turns the drift term into $K|Z_s|$, which feeds Grönwall's lemma.
The divergent integral gives the levels $a_k$ and the weights $\varphi_k \le 2/(k\rho^2)$ that cancel $\rho^2$ in the Itô correction.
With the same Brownian motion the difference $Z = X - Y$ has a single stochastic integral, and $Z_0 = 0$.

steps.slogan: Build $C^2$ approximations $\psi_k$ of $|w|$ with small second derivative weighted by $\rho^2$.
steps.detail: Choose $a_k \downarrow 0$ with $\int_{a_k}^{a_{k-1}} \rho^{-2} = k$ and a continuous $\varphi_k \le 2/(k\rho^2)$ on $(a_k, a_{k-1})$ with integral 1. Then $\psi_k(w) = \int_0^{|w|}\int_0^v \varphi_k$ satisfies $|\psi_k'| \le 1$, $\psi_k'' = \varphi_k(|w|)$ and $|w| - a_{k-1} \le \psi_k(w) \le |w|$.

steps.slogan: Write the difference $Z = X - Y$ and stop it at the exit [stopping time](c:stopping-time) $\tau$.
steps.detail: With $\tau = \inf\{t : |Z_t| \ge \gamma\}$ the hypotheses apply up to $\tau$, so the drift difference is at most $K|Z_s|$ and the diffusion difference at most $\rho(|Z_s|) \le \rho(\gamma)$.

steps.slogan: Expand $\psi_k(Z_{t\wedge\tau})$ by Itô's formula and remove the bounded [martingale](c:martingale) part.
steps.detail: Itô's formula gives a stochastic integral with integrand bounded by $\rho(\gamma)$ plus a drift integral with integrand $\psi_k'(Z)\beta + \frac12\varphi_k(|Z|)\alpha^2$. The Itô isometry makes the stochastic integral a martingale with [expected value](c:expected-value) 0.

steps.slogan: Bound the Itô correction by $1/k$ and the drift term by $K|Z_s|$.
steps.detail: Where $\varphi_k(|Z_s|) \ne 0$, the bound $\varphi_k \le 2/(k\rho^2)$ and $\alpha_s^2 \le \rho(|Z_s|)^2$ give $\frac12\varphi_k\alpha_s^2 \le 1/k$. Hence $E\psi_k(Z_{t\wedge\tau}) \le t/k + K\int_0^t E|Z_{s\wedge\tau}|\,ds$.

steps.slogan: Let $k \to \infty$ and close the integral inequality with Grönwall's lemma.
steps.detail: With $u(t) = E|Z_{t\wedge\tau}|$ the bound $\psi_k(w) \ge |w| - a_{k-1}$ gives $u(t) \le a_{k-1} + t/k + K\int_0^t u$. In the limit $u(t) \le K\int_0^t u(s)\,ds$, and Grönwall's lemma gives $u \equiv 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that $Z$ never reaches level $\gamma$ and vanishes at all times.
steps.detail: On $\{\tau \le t\}$ the stopped difference has absolute value $\gamma > 0$, so $P(\tau \le t) = 0$ and $Z_t = 0$ almost surely. Rational times and continuity of paths give indistinguishability.

new_concepts.name: pathwise uniqueness
new_concepts.reminder: Pathwise uniqueness means that two solutions driven by the same Brownian motion from the same start agree almost surely.
new_concepts.definition: A [stochastic differential equation](c:stochastic-differential-equation) $dX_t=b(t,X_t)\,dt+\sigma(t,X_t)\,dB_t$ has pathwise uniqueness when, for any two solutions $X$ and $X'$ on a common filtered probability space with the same [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $B$ and $X_0=X'_0$ almost surely, $P(X_t=X'_t\text{ for all }t\ge0)=1$. By the Yamada–Watanabe theorem, weak existence and pathwise uniqueness together give a unique [strong solution](c:strong-solution) and uniqueness in law.

statement: If the coefficients $\sigma$ and $b$ are [Lipschitz](c:lipschitz-continuous-function) in space uniformly in time, then the [stochastic differential equation](c:stochastic-differential-equation) $dX_t = \sigma(t, X_t)\,dB_t + b(t, X_t)\,dt$ has [pathwise uniqueness](c:pathwise-uniqueness), and for every starting point it has a [strong solution](c:strong-solution).

hypotheses.text: There is $K$ with $\|\sigma(t,x) - \sigma(t,y)\| \le K|x-y|$ and $|b(t,x) - b(t,y)| \le K|x-y|$ for all $t, x, y$, so the coefficients are [Lipschitz](c:lipschitz-continuous-function) in space uniformly in time.
The values $\|\sigma(t,0)\|$ and $|b(t,0)|$ are bounded on every interval $[0,T]$.
$B$ is an $m$-dimensional [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) with respect to a complete [filtration](c:filtration).

conclusion: Two solutions with the same Brownian motion and equal initial values are indistinguishable, and for each $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ there is a solution with $X_0 = x$, adapted to the filtration of $B$, with $\mathbb{E}\sup_{t \le T}|X_t|^2 < \infty$.

proofs.name: Localization for uniqueness and Picard iteration for existence
proofs.slogan: One maximal $L^2$ estimate gives uniqueness through Grönwall's lemma and a factorial bound for the Picard iterates.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for deterministic initial values $x$ in every dimension.

roles.why: The Lipschitz bound turns differences of coefficients into differences of solutions in the key estimate.
It bounds the coefficients along the constant path $x$, so the first Picard increment has a finite second moment.
The [Itô integral](c:ito-integral) against $B$ is a [martingale](c:martingale) to which Doob's inequality and the Itô isometry apply.

steps.slogan: Bound the stopped maximal distance of two Itô processes by an integral of their mean square distance.
steps.detail: For a [stopping time](c:stopping-time) $\tau$, Doob's $L^2$ inequality, the Itô isometry and Cauchy-Schwarz give $\mathbb{E}\sup_{s\le t}|\tilde X_{s\wedge\tau} - \tilde Y_{s\wedge\tau}|^2 \le 3\mathbb{E}|\tilde X_0 - \tilde Y_0|^2 + 3(4+t)K^2\int_0^t \mathbb{E}|X_{r\wedge\tau} - Y_{r\wedge\tau}|^2\,dr$.

steps.slogan: Localize two solutions in a ball and close the estimate with Grönwall's lemma.
steps.detail: With $\tau$ the exit time of either solution from the ball of radius $M$, the function $g(t) = \mathbb{E}\sup_{s\le t}|X_{s\wedge\tau} - X'_{s\wedge\tau}|^2$ is bounded and satisfies $g \le C_T\int_0^t g$, so $g = 0$. Letting $M \to \infty$ gives indistinguishability.

steps.slogan: Build Picard iterates and bound their increments by a factorial sequence.
steps.detail: With $X^0 = x$ and $X^{n+1} = x + \int \sigma(s, X^n_s)\,dB_s + \int b(s, X^n_s)\,ds$, the estimate gives $g_{n+1}(t) \le C_T\int_0^t g_n$ for $g_n(t) = \mathbb{E}\sup_{s\le t}|X^n_s - X^{n-1}_s|^2$, hence $g_n(t) \le C'_T C_T^{n-1}t^{n-1}/(n-1)!$.

steps.slogan: Sum the increments to get uniform almost sure and mean square convergence of the iterates.
steps.detail: The square roots of the factorial bounds are summable, so $\sum_n \sup_{t\le T}|X^{n+1}_t - X^n_t|$ has finite mean. The iterates converge uniformly on $[0,T]$ almost surely and in $L^2$ of the supremum norm to a continuous adapted limit $X$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the limit in the recursion to show that the limit is a strong solution.
steps.detail: The Lipschitz bound with Cauchy-Schwarz and the Itô isometry show that both integrals in the recursion converge in $L^2$. So $X$ satisfies the equation for each $t$, then for all $t$ by continuity, and it is a [strong solution](c:strong-solution) of the [stochastic differential equation](c:stochastic-differential-equation).

concepts.c:lipschitz-continuous-function: The Lipschitz bound on the coefficients drives every estimate of the proof.
concepts.c:stochastic-differential-equation: The theorem is about solutions of this stochastic differential equation.
concepts.c:pathwise-uniqueness: Pathwise uniqueness is the first conclusion, proved by localization and Grönwall.
concepts.c:strong-solution: The Picard limit is adapted to the Brownian filtration, so it is a strong solution.
concepts.c:brownian-motion: The Brownian motion drives the equation and the stochastic integrals.
concepts.c:filtration: Solutions are adapted to a complete filtration for which B is a Brownian motion.
concepts.c:ito-integral: The noise term of the equation is an Itô integral against B.
concepts.c:martingale: Stopped stochastic integrals are martingales, so Doob's inequality applies.
concepts.c:stopping-time: The exit time from a ball localizes the solutions in the uniqueness proof.

source.ref: R. Lyons, Stochastic Calculus, lecture notes based on Le Gall's book (version of August 23, 2026), Theorem 8.3 and Lemma 8A, pp. 106-108.

new_concepts.name: strong solution of a stochastic differential equation
new_concepts.reminder: A strong solution of a stochastic differential equation is built from the given Brownian motion and initial value alone.
new_concepts.definition: Fix a probability space with a [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $B$, an initial value $\xi$ independent of $B$, and the [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal{F}_t)$ that $\xi$ and $B$ generate, augmented by the null sets. A strong solution of the [stochastic differential equation](c:stochastic-differential-equation) $dX_t=b(t,X_t)\,dt+\sigma(t,X_t)\,dB_t$ with $X_0=\xi$ is a continuous process $X$ adapted to $(\mathcal{F}_t)$ such that both integrals exist and $X_t=\xi+\int_0^tb(s,X_s)\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma(s,X_s)\,dB_s$ for all $t$, almost surely. A weak solution, in contrast, can use a Brownian motion and a filtration that are constructed together with $X$.

statement: If the diffusion matrix $a$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) and positive definite and the drift $b$ is [measurable](c:measurable-function), with linear growth conditions, then the [martingale](c:martingale) problem for the [elliptic operator](c:elliptic-operator) $L_s$ has exactly one solution from every starting point, and the solutions form a [Markov process](c:markov-chain).

hypotheses.text: The diffusion matrix $a(s,x)$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function), symmetric and positive definite, with $|a_{ij}(s,x)| \le C(1+|x|^2)$.
The drift $b(s,x)$ is [measurable](c:measurable-function) with $|b_i(s,x)| \le C(1+|x|)$.

conclusion: For every $(s_0, x_0)$ there is exactly one law $P_{s_0,x_0}$ on continuous paths that solves the martingale problem from $(s_0, x_0)$, and $p(s,x,t,A) = P_{s,x}[x(t)\in A]$ is its transition probability.

proofs.name: Localization, Girsanov and perturbation of the heat equation
proofs.slogan: Freeze the continuous diffusion matrix near each point, solve the frozen problem by perturbing the heat equation in $L^p$, and patch the local uniqueness together.
proofs.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 14.3 in Varadhan's Spring 2011 notes, with Lemmas 14.1 and 14.2.

roles.why: Continuity lets the matrix stay close to a constant near each point, which the perturbation needs, and positive definiteness gives uniform ellipticity on compact sets.
Boundedness on balls lets Girsanov's theorem remove the drift, and linear growth keeps the solution from exploding.

steps.slogan: Solve the parabolic equation for nearly constant $a$ by a Neumann series around the heat equation.
steps.detail: With the heat Green operator $G$ built from the [fundamental solution](c:fundamental-solution) and Jones's bound $\|u_t\|_p + \sum\|u_{ij}\|_p \le C_p\|f\|_p$, with $(Gg)_s + \frac12\Delta(Gg) = -g$, the series $u = -G(I - \frac12[a-I](G\cdot)_{ij})^{-1}f$ converges when $\sup|a_{ij}-\delta_{ij}|$ is small. It gives $u$ in the [Sobolev space](c:sobolev-space) $W^{1,2}_p$ with $\sup|u| \le c(T)\|f\|_p$.

steps.slogan: Identify the occupation integrals of every solution with the PDE solution $u$.
steps.detail: Itô's formula for $u$ gives $E^P\int_{s_0}^T f(t,x(t))\,dt = -u(s_0,x_0)$ for every solution $P$, so the one-dimensional laws agree. Conditional laws of a solution are again solutions, which fixes all finite-dimensional laws.

steps.slogan: Patch local uniqueness along successive exit times into global uniqueness.
steps.detail: Two solutions agree up to the exit [stopping time](c:stopping-time) from a small neighbourhood, because after it both can be continued by the unique local solution. Induction over exit times $\tau_n \to \infty$ gives $P_1 = P_2$ (Lemma 14.1).

steps.slogan: Remove a bounded drift with Girsanov's change of measure.
steps.detail: For uniformly elliptic $a$ and bounded $b$, the density $\exp(\int\langle a^{-1}b, dx\rangle - \frac12\int\langle b, a^{-1}b\rangle ds)$ maps solutions for $[a,0]$ one-to-one onto solutions for $[a,b]$.

steps.slogan: Reduce general coefficients to bounded ones by modifying them outside large balls.
steps.detail: Every solution agrees with the solution for the modified coefficients up to the exit time $\tau_\ell$ from the ball of radius $\ell$, and $\tau_\ell \to \infty$ by continuity of paths. So uniqueness needs no growth condition.

steps.slogan: Prove non-explosion with the Lyapunov function $1+|x|^2$ and pass to the limit.
steps.detail: The growth bounds give $L_s(1+|x|^2) \le C'(1+|x|^2)$, so $E[e^{-C'\tau_\ell}] \le (1+|x_0|^2)/(1+\ell^2)$. The solutions $P^\ell$ then agree on larger and larger events and converge to a solution, which is unique and [Markov](c:markov-chain).

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity of the diffusion matrix lets the proof freeze it near each point.
concepts.c:measurable-function: The drift only needs to be measurable, because Girsanov's theorem removes it.
concepts.c:martingale: A solution is a law under which every test function gives a martingale.
concepts.c:elliptic-operator: The generator is a second-order elliptic operator with a positive definite matrix.
concepts.c:markov-chain: Uniqueness from every starting point makes the solutions a Markov process.
concepts.c:fundamental-solution: The heat kernel gives the Green operator around which the proof perturbs.
concepts.c:sobolev-space: The perturbed parabolic equation has a solution in a Sobolev space of $L^p$ derivatives.
concepts.c:stopping-time: Exit times from small neighbourhoods are the stopping times along which local uniqueness is patched.
